    The developers of One-armed Robber are asking players to spend their surprise refunds in the free Steam heist game after a hacker sent the money back without the studio’s permission.

    Duhndal released One-armed Robber in December 2023. The first-person game lets players rob banks and stores solo or with friends, with each robber limited to one arm. Crews can sneak into a vault or fight their way through, then haul out as much loot as they can carry. The game has roughly 54,000 Steam reviews, according to SteamDB.

    On November 20, Duhndal stated someone gained access to one of its Steamworks API keys and used it to ban players and matter refunds for in-game purchases. The studio said the incident affected a small share of its player base.

    The refunds went to players who had never asked for their money back. Duhndal said the transactions caused “significant financial losses” for its small team. The studio gave no figure for the losses or how many refunds were issued.

    It has been revealed that duhndal asked players who want to help it recover to put some of their refund toward another purchase in One-armed Robber or one of the studio’s other games. It also declared a sale on heist maps for players looking to pick up missions they don’t already own.

    In a recent development, “This is completely optional! You haven’t done anything wrong, and you don’t owe us anything,” the developer said.

    According to recent reports, duhndal said it revoked the compromised key and lifted all unauthorized bans. Players who were unfairly banned should now be able to get back into the game.

    The viral story of a grandmother who accidentally invited a stranger to Thanksgiving dinner is being turned into a Lifetime movie, nearly 10 years after their unlikely friendship began.

    Wanda Dench and Jamal Hinton first made headlines in 2016 when a mistaken text message led to the pair celebrating Thanksgiving together. What started as an accidental invitation has since become an annual tradition, with the two continuing to reunite for the holiday.

    Now, their friendship is heading to television after the pair signed a deal with Lifetime to bring their story to the screen, with a movie expected to arrive in November 2027.

    Dench confirmed to The Arizona Republic on November 16 that she and Hinton recently signed over the rights to their story for a Lifetime movie right now titled ‘The Thanksgiving Grandma.’.

    The film is expected to begin production in early 2027, with producer Jack Leslie targeting a November release that same year.

    “They did tell us right up front that it’s based on our story,” Dench explained.

    Hinton also declared the news on Instagram, sharing a photo alongside Dench and celebrating their partnership with Lifetime.

    Industry observers note that “Very excited to officially be in business with Lifetime!” he wrote. “They believe in our story, and it truly feels like we’re in the best hands as we take this next step.”.

    He also thanked Dench for being a constant source of support throughout their friendship, telling followers that their journey was only getting started.

    It has been revealed that the pair’s story began in November 2016 when Dench accidentally texted Hinton while attempting to invite her grandson to Thanksgiving dinner. Unbeknownst to her, her grandson had changed his phone number, and Hinton received the invitation instead.

    After exchanging messages and photos, the two realized they were strangers. However, Hinton jokingly asked whether he could still attend dinner.

    “Of course you can, that’s what grandmas do … feed everyone,” Dench responded.

    Their exchange promptly went viral on Twitter, and Hinton ultimately joined Dench and her family for Thanksgiving at her home in Arizona.

    The tradition has continued every year since, with the pair sharing updates about their friendship on social media.

    The upcoming Lifetime movie has been in development in various forms for years. Leslie initially approached Dench about adapting the story in 2018 while working at Netflix, but the project was eventually abandoned following downsizing at the company.

    Screenwriter Glen Dolman is now working on the Lifetime adaptation and recently spent a weekend at Dench’s home to learn more about their relationship.

    “It’s going to be more of how we’ve supported each other throughout the 10 years,” Dench explained.

    YouTube ‘Co-Views’ try to guess how many people are watching your TV, rolling out now

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (396 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.
    • View counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays.
    • Now, YouTube claims it might count more views with a fresh “Co-Views” setup on TVs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.

    View counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays. But, even with that, YouTube only counts a single view for each time the video is played.

    Now, YouTube claims it might count more views with a fresh “Co-Views” setup on TVs.

    In a post, YouTube explains that “Co-Views” include “the estimated number of people watching together on TV” in the view count of a video. This only applies to TVs, with views from a mobile device or desktop still only ever counting as a single video. It applies to long-form videos as well as Shorts and Live videos, and only applies going forward – historical data won’t change.

    YouTube indicates it is making this change to reflect the “over 1 billion hours” spend on YouTube through their TVs “every day” and that the added data will assist creators in channel strategy or brand pitches, while also providing a “more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with’ content, aligning with TV industry standards – including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.” But “Co-Views” won’t count towards earnings on the platform, as they’re not “Qualified Views.”.

    How is YouTube figuring out what to count here? “Guessing” is not exactly an inaccurate summarization, but Google stresses that it is not using cameras or microphones, but rather a “statistical mode.”.

    YouTube doesn’t use devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that. Co-views are estimated using a privacy safe statistical mode, developed by Google research scientists, based on factors like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against ground-truth data sources like industry panels.

    This change is rolling out now.

The smaller, dense Qwen 3.6 27B manages about 24 tokens per second on the same platform, and the V100s use about half the energy of the same number of P100s for a given job.

    It has been revealed that the blog post, “Scaling ‘E-Waste’: LLMs on Multiple Decommissioned GPUs,” compares nine different builds — one to three K80s, P100s, or V100-16GB cards — on a single Supermicro dual-Xeon board. The test uses llama.cpp and covers more than 130 LLM tests, including Qwen 2.5, Gemma 4, and, of course, Qwen 3.6, at Q4/Q8/F16 precisions and from 4K to 128K context sizes. GPU energy per run is also recorded. The builder is “daily driving Qwen 3.6 35B” on the V100s and notes that scaling decommissioned GPUs will only get you so far.

    It has been revealed that “E-waste,” in this case, refers to decommissioned enterprise GPUs, which are a popular but somewhat underpowered option when compared to very expensive modern alternatives. The Nvidia Tesla V100s in question are tested as a follow-up to a July round which tested 15 “e-waste” GPUs, and this time the board and CPUs stay the same for every build — the Supermicro X10DRG-Q with two Intel Xeon E5-2687W 12-core CPUs, powered by the Corsair HX1500i PSU.

    Sources indicate that performance is judged based on what is considered “realtime interaction” which, here, is 70 tokens per second. As to why the number of GPUs is three: Qwen 3.6 35B, the primary tested model, fails on just one or two at Q8, or 8-bit quantization.

    Here are the given prices, with the note that they aren’t “100% reflective of what you could find on eBay today,” although the totals count only one of the two CPUs and omit RAM, storage, the case, and any cooling.

    The older cards are relatively inexpensive because they “run hot and ship without cooling,” which required the builder to 3D print one blower duct per card and has led to the development of a standalone cooler.

    Recent findings suggest that the bench itself involves 10 runs of 512 generated tokens per test with context pre-filled to 4K, 32K, 64K, or 128K. Qwen 3.6 35B is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, which only activates about 3 billion out of its 35 billion total parameters per token. The numbers that immediately follow are at Q8.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    The token goal was easily reached…when the context window was small, or 4K. The 100.8 tokens per second there fell to 72.7 at 128K, still usable by the 70 tokens per second goal. The 27B model, which is not MoE, fared much worse, at 24.3 at 4K, 21.6 at 32K, 18.7 at 64K, and just 14.2 at 128K. The MoE ends up about four to five times faster, depending on the context size.

    Also tested were other dense models of about 30B parameters. At 4K, Gemma 4 31B achieved 20.9 and Qwen 2.5 32B 21.0, while the MoE Gemma 4 26B cleared the 70 tokens per second bar with just two V100s at Q8. If you move down to Q4, or 4-bit quantization, two V100s can run Qwen 3.6 35B at 77.1 to 105.4 tokens per second, between 128K and 4K context size. This is where it’s claimed that adding more cards gives you more memory, which enables larger models to be run, but not speed.

    The P100s, for comparison, only hit 40.2–55.2 tokens per second in the same context range with Q8 Qwen 3.6 35B, and the target 70 only with Qwen 2.5 3B. If we compare to more modern hardware — the Nvidia DGX Spark, MSRP $4,700, and the M5 Max Mac Studio, which starts at $2,499 but costs $5,399 with the tested 40-core GPU, 128GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD — the 3x V100 build holds its own, using sourced data.

    In a recent development, the Mac comparison comes from the oMLX benchmark page for the M5 Max with 40 GPU cores and 128GB of unified memory, and that hits 43.9 tokens per second with a ~195K-token prompt on the Qwen 3.6 35B model. The Mac is slightly ahead at 4K and 32K, while the V100s pull ahead at 64K and 128K, by 19% at the longest context. These numbers have to be taken loosely, as the machines use different runtimes.

    Sources indicate that the Spark run came from Kleybrink’s dgx-spark-bench, using Ollama in thinking mode with short prompts. Its 45.8 tokens per second is less than half the V100s’ 4K figure.

    According to recent reports, going further to modern GPUs, which “destroy our decommissioned equivalents,” as the builder puts it, you get about 315 tokens per second on two H100s and about 455 on one B200 at 128K, the B200 roughly six times the V100 box, even though the hosted cards ran the full 16-bit model against the V100s’ 8-bit. Parasail, an inference provider, sponsored that comparison with dedicated H100 and B200 deployments.

    It has been revealed that as for energy, the V100 setup came out to about 0.02 kWh for a 128K 35B run, with the P100s taking twice that much and two or three K80s as much as 0.35 to 0.45 kWh. The V100-16GB simply “[puts] up better scores while consuming less energy,” in comparison to the P100s. These numbers are for the GPUs and not from the wall.

    There’s more to come. The builder wants a benchmark that “maps to ‘software factory’ performance,” a term for models being prompted constantly, around the clock, where instant speed matters less. Then there’s the cooler, which is “almost ready for release,” with beta testers to be recruited from the mailing list, although no date has been given. From the Reddit thread, the builder mentions the intention to compare inference backends and use speculative decoding to improve performance.

    Taco Bell is bringing back a discontinued menu item after a decade, with the fast-food chain confirming that one of its former burritos will return to restaurants nationwide in 2027.

    The announcement comes as Taco Bell continues to revive older menu items, including the Quesarito, Flamin’ Hot Grilled Cheese Burrito, and Cheesy Street Chalupas, which have recently returned for limited-time runs.

    According to recent reports, however, the latest comeback wasn’t decided by Taco Bell executives. Instead, the company allowed fans to choose which discontinued item would return as part of its inaugural Live Más Open golf tournament, hosted by comedian Kevin Hart.

    Taco Bell has confirmed that the Steakhouse Boss Burrito will return to participating US restaurants for a limited time in 2027, marking its first appearance since 2016.

    Originally introduced as the Steakhouse Burrito, the returning item features a warm flour tortilla filled with a choice of grilled, marinated steak or marinated all-white-meat chicken.

    The burrito includes twice the amount of meat found in Taco Bell’s Steak Grilled Cheese Burrito, along with warm queso sauce, bacon, seasoned potatoes, and reduced-fat sour cream.

    It also features a three-cheese blend consisting of mozzarella, pepper jack, and cheddar.

    The decision to bring back the burrito came during Taco Bell’s Live Más Open, which took place at The Ranch at Laguna Beach in California earlier this month.

    The nine-hole golf tournament featured celebrities, athletes, and Taco Bell fans competing for the opportunity to revive a discontinued menu item.

    Team Pink, consisting of Taco Bell fan Abby Abel, professional skateboarder Sean Malto, influencer Emira D’Spain, and reality television personality Serena Page, secured the victory following a sudden-death putting playoff against Team White.

    Taco Bell is making fans win a golf tournament to bring back a discontinued menu item.

    Taco Bell quietly tests Fire Piña Hot Dog on exclusive secret menu.

    Taco Bell revives Shredded Beef Dipping Taco alongside latest beef loaded Nacho Fries.

    Their prize included championship jackets, a trophy, and the opportunity to select a former Taco Bell menu item for a nationwide comeback.

    The tournament also featured a Taco Bell drive-thru on the golf course, serving exclusive items including the Fire Piña Hot Dog, Baja Caesar Crispy Chicken Crunchwrap, and Fiesta Potato Salad.

    The Live Más Open is available to stream on Peacock beginning November 20, with a television broadcast scheduled for November 23 on Golf Channel.

    Taco Bell has not confirmed an exact release date or pricing for the Steakhouse Boss Burrito, although the manufacturer confirmed it will be available nationwide for a limited time in 2027.

    The announcement follows several other menu changes from Taco Bell, including the return of the Quesarito and the upcoming Make It Flamin’ Hot customization option, which will allow customers to add Flamin’ Hot Fritos to eligible menu items beginning November 24.

    Latest Update: Ukraine deploys homemade 'flying modems' in daring drone attack to destroy Crimean Bridge, ditching Elon Musk's Starlink

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that ukrainian forces ditched Elon Musk's Starlink wireless system and used their own relay network of "flying modems" to maintain a live feed of an attack on the Crimean Bridge, even amid Russian attempts to block the signal.
    • In a recent development, videos of the attack showed Flamingo missiles, carrying a 1,200kg warhead, being remotely piloted towards the bridge.
    • Industry observers note that with Starlink, or Starshield, no longer fit for Ukraine's needs, it turned to the "flying drones" instead.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that ukrainian forces ditched Elon Musk's Starlink wireless system and used their own relay network of "flying modems" to maintain a live feed of an attack on the Crimean Bridge, even amid Russian attempts to block the signal. The attack, which led to the partial collapse of the bridge, was significant for a number of reasons. The bridge is one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most symbolic assets due to its linking of the occupied Crimean Peninsula and Russia. But perhaps more importantly, the attack's use of Ukrainian connectivity technology highlights the country's lessening of its reliance on Starlink. The modems were crucial to the success of the mission, with the FT reporting that they kept missiles connected to their pilots while they manoeuvred through Russia's air defenses.

    In a recent development, videos of the attack showed Flamingo missiles, carrying a 1,200kg warhead, being remotely piloted towards the bridge. Flamingo missiles are capable of traveling at around 590 miles per hour, requiring a stable and reliable video feed. It's reported that the Ukrainians deliberately chose not to use Starshield, the military version of Musk's Starlink, for the operation, with the company's satellite network having been restricted in recent weeks. That restricted service would have been insufficient for the Crimean Bridge attack, forcing Ukrainian forces to find another solution. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy remarked this week that he has not been told why Starlink's connection has been throttled, with neither the White House nor the Pentagon being forthcoming. SpaceX, Starlink's parent company, has also so far not provided any explanation. However, relations between Zelenskyy and Musk appear to be strained, with the SpaceX CEO saying that Ukraine had "gone too far" by striking Russian data centers.

    Industry observers note that with Starlink, or Starshield, no longer fit for Ukraine's needs, it turned to the "flying drones" instead. The flying communications towers were used as a relay, boosting the signal sent from individual missiles so that it could more readily reach their pilots. This approach allowed the weapons to fly farther while still maintaining a reliable connection, allowing them to bypass Russian air defense systems and attempts to block their signals in the process. Without the relays, Ukrainian drone pilots have previously had to program missiles with coordinates and then rely on their autopilot system. They were inevitably shot down because they could not be steered away from Russian defenses.

    Perhaps ironically, Ukraine isn't the first country to use flying communications towers. Russian forces were using similar technology as early as 2023, before the system began using a Chinese mesh networking system.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly. Most interesting was a running server at the CXL booth, showcasing a demo with a Diamond Rapids CPU. The server ran for the first day of the show, and upon returning to the booth, we were informed that it had been shut down due to noise complaints (it’s hard to mistake a running server). Elsewhere at Bull’s booth, a Diamond Rapids CPU was shown installed in a server behind a glass case. Notably, Intel didn’t have a Diamond Rapids demo, instead focusing most of its booth on Xeon 6+ and its new D270 GPU, otherwise known as Crescent Island.

    The demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller. If you’re unfamiliar, memory expansion via CXL is an increasingly common tactic to give multi-host environments access to a large pool of memory, breaking free of an individual server’s capacity via CXL. In the demo, Montage is showing off its memory expansion controller running across a Xeon 6 and a Diamond Rapids server, each sharing a pool of memory over CXL. CXL is an open standard, built atop PCIe.

    Recent findings suggest that of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild. The 256 GB memory capacity shown doesn’t provide any hints, either. Intel has revealed that Diamond Rapids will support 16-channel memory, with RDIMM support up to 8,000 MT/s and MRDIMM support up to 12,800 MT/s, matching AMD’s recent EPYC Venice CPUs. However, Intel hasn’t revealed capacity, though we anticipate the maximum capacity will be far above 256 GB – for context, last-gen Granite Rapids-AP supports up to 3 TB per socket.

    Sources indicate that bull is a French server designer focused on HPC and AI infrastructure, and it showed off two Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids chips installed in the Bullsquana XH31600 server. As expected for a 2P Diamond Rapids server, it supports 32 channels of DDR5 memory, and it’s designed for a liquid-cooled deployment.

    In a recent development, as you can see from the image, these aren’t production chips. They’re labeled with “Intel confidential,” and the code starts with “Q,” revealing that this is a sample. Originally, we expected to see Diamond Rapids in the second half of this year, perhaps around this time. However, in August, Intel revealed that Xeon 7 chips would launch in 2027.

    Based on the various servers we saw and the live demo, it seems Intel is targeting a launch earlier in the year, likely in Q2; we expect a larger consumer focus in Q1. It could slip later into the year, though that seems very unlikely given that Diamond Rapids was already pushed back, and the insatiable demand for CPUs in AI data centers doesn’t appear to be drying up.

    In a recent development, also pointing to a relatively quick release are the various servers we saw on the floor at SC26. Several partners demonstrated off their next-gen servers built for Diamond Rapids CPU, sporting the LGA 9324 socket, including Dell and Asus (pictured above). However, Bull was the only vendor we could find that had an actual chip on display.

    Diamond Rapids is Intel’s true next-gen CPU, following up on the E-core-only Xeon 6+ range that launched earlier this year. Diamond Rapids packs up to 256 P-cores, and it’s built on Intel’s performance-enhanced 18A-P node. The most interesting aspect of the chip is its topology, with Intel breaking from its previous layout and building something much similar to an EPYC CPU. The package features centralized memory and I/O, which were pushed out to the edges of the package with Granite Rapids. You can read more about the design of the chip in our Diamond Rapids recap from Hot Chips on Tom’s Hardware Premium.

    Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

    The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a new Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone?

    In a recent development, meta introduced its own-branded smart glasses this summer (read: with no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding), and they seem to have done well for a number of reasons. Some models are much cheaper than Ray-Ban-branded pairs, while other Meta glasses carry Kylie Jenner or LISA names, bringing in a unique note of fashion, but none of these models changed the look of the camera LED indicator on the front.

    Sources indicate that meta has come under fire over the past two years as people have abused the manufacturer’s smart glasses, giving them the unfortunate term “perv glasses” on social media because some people disabled the camera LED, which is supposed to illuminate when the camera is recording. Meta has issued several different software patches to disable the glasses’ camera when the LED is tampered with, but many have begun to feel like having a camera on smart glasses just feels wrong after people have abused the technology.

    Meta glasses product lead David Woodland posted a render of the Gentle Monster cateye style glasses in a now-deleted Tweet on X on November 17, simply saying “I plead the fifth.” Presumably, he was calling out how similar these glasses look to the Meta Starfire Kylie Jenner style, but we’ll likely never know now.

    Samsung and Google’s Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses certainly resemble Meta’s glasses, but they also do something noticeably different: the camera LED doesn’t look like the camera on the other side.

    Industry observers note that so this begs the question: can Meta do anything to salvage the unsavory association its glasses now have attached to them? We covered this topic on episode 125 of our Pixelated podcast, and Woodland’s post further highlights the question. A camera LED that’s obviously different from the camera on the other side would likely prompt people to ask about your glasses, while Meta’s design is purposefully stealthy because of its symmetry.

    It has been revealed that does this design difference help Samsung’s Gentle Monster/Warby Parker glasses feel more private, and would a similar redesign help Meta’s glasses? I think it would help a lot, but I also want to know what our readers think. What say you, folks?

    Silicon Motion demos SM8466 PCIe 6.0 SSD controller, expected to ship by 2028 — controller boasts improved quality of service, samples imminent

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Silicon Motion is showing off its PCIe 6.0 SSD controller for data center applications for the first time at the SC26 conference in Chicago.
    • Silicon Motion introduced its high-end MonTitan SM8466 enterprise SSD controller designed for next-generation data center and hyperscale storage applications at FMS 2025.
    • To improve performance and reduce latency, Silicon Motion has developed its Separate Command Architecture (SCA), which separates command and address transmission paths within the NAND interface to improve parallelism and increase effective throughput.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Silicon Motion is showing off its PCIe 6.0 SSD controller for data center applications for the first time at the SC26 conference in Chicago. The final iteration of Silicon Motion's SM8466 controller was taped out recently, and drives based on the chip are due in late 2027 or early 2028. However, the latest controller also has a secret weapon designed to ensure consistent performance of SSDs under concurrent workloads that may set it apart from competitors.

    Silicon Motion introduced its high-end MonTitan SM8466 enterprise SSD controller designed for next-generation data center and hyperscale storage applications at FMS 2025. The controller features a PCIe 6.x x4 host interface and 16 NAND channels to enable sequential transfer speeds of up to 28 GB/s, random performance of up to 7 million 4K IOPS, and capacities of up to 512 TB and beyond as newer 3D NAND devices emerge. Just like other high-end data center-grade SSD controllers released in recent years, the SM8466 complies with NVMe 2.0 and OCP NVMe 2.5 SSD specifications.

    To improve performance and reduce latency, Silicon Motion has developed its Separate Command Architecture (SCA), which separates command and address transmission paths within the NAND interface to improve parallelism and increase effective throughput. Additionally, the controller supports Silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology, which enables programmable performance limits and predictable quality of service (QoS) across concurrent workloads, which is arguably its most important differentiator against rivals who rely on different methods of guaranteeing performance.

    It has been revealed that in addition to its performance chops, the MonTitan SM8466 incorporates advanced error correction, virtualization, data protection, and security features. The controller's error correction engine supports low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with 4KiB codewords and Silicon Motion's 16KiB Collaborative Codeword (CoCo) technology to improve data integrity and reliability with advanced NAND flash memory. The controller also supports Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV), MPF virtualization, SMART diagnostics, and comprehensive data protection mechanisms. Security capabilities include Secure Boot, AES-256 encryption, TCG Opal compatibility, and firmware attestation. Together, these features make the SM8466 suitable for high-capacity data center drives that are expected to deliver high performance, predictable latency, and reliable operation under demanding data center workloads.

    Silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology builds upon the original PerformaShape architecture introduced with the company's PCIe 5.0-based MonTitan SM8366 enterprise SSD controller several years ago. The 1st Generation implementation uses dedicated hardware accelerators and two-stage leaky-bucket regulators to control read and write performance in terms of IOPS and throughput, both for individual workloads and for the SSD as a whole. This approach enables data center operators to prevent one workload from monopolizing SSD resources at the expense of others.

    PerformaShape 2 retains these capabilities but doubles the number of supported quality-of-service (QoS) sets from 256 to 512 and introduces more sophisticated performance controls to accommodate a larger number of concurrent workloads with different requirements. One of the key additions to PerformaShape 2 is Multi-Dimensional Shaping, which enables the controller to coordinate performance limits across multiple I/O characteristics rather than enforce each limit independently. This gives data center operators greater flexibility when allocating SSD resources among applications with different performance requirements.

    Sources indicate that another notable enhancement of PerformaShape 2 is support for NVMe TP4176, a proposed extension to the NVMe specification that aims to standardize performance management and QoS controls. Whereas the original PerformaShape relies on Silicon Motion's vendor-specific NVMe commands and a dedicated host driver, TP4176 could eventually enable compatible host software to configure performance policies through a standardized mechanism. The technology is particularly relevant for cloud environments where SSDs serve numerous virtual machines, containers, and applications whose storage requirements can change considerably over time, according to the company.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A North Carolina woman was evicted from her apartment after an AI leasing assistant mistakenly told her she could delay paying nearly $4,000 in overdue rent.
    • Laura Mack, a resident of Colony Townhome Apartments in Raleigh, received an email on November 8 asking when she could pay her outstanding balance of $3,934.17.
    • Mack responded that she wanted to pay on November 30 and received written confirmation that the date was acceptable.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A North Carolina woman was evicted from her apartment after an AI leasing assistant mistakenly told her she could delay paying nearly $4,000 in overdue rent.

    Laura Mack, a resident of Colony Townhome Apartments in Raleigh, received an email on November 8 asking when she could pay her outstanding balance of $3,934.17.

    Mack responded that she wanted to pay on November 30 and received written confirmation that the date was acceptable. However, eight days later, she was served with an eviction notice.

    When Mack contacted the leasing office, she said an employee explained that the emails had been sent by Olivia, the apartment complex’s AI assistant, which had mistakenly approved her request.

    The complex had introduced Olivia to residents in December 2025, explaining that the assistant could answer questions about rent and maintenance around the clock.

    Although previous emails from Olivia had been clearly identified as AI-generated, the November 8 messages were signed by Colony Townhome Apartments and did not disclose that they had been written by a chatbot.

    Mack stated she believed she was communicating with a member of staff, particularly because the emails referenced a bathroom ceiling leak that had taken almost two weeks to repair.

    “I thought it was someone from the office because all my information was in there and it mentioned my bathroom,” she told WRAL.

    Industry observers note that despite having the agreement in writing, Mack was evicted on November 19. She subsequently stayed in a hotel while trying to determine her next steps.

    “If you told me till the 30th, I’ll get out by the 30th,” she said. “But give me that. You at least honor that. You have to have somewhere where you’re taking responsibility.”.

    Recent findings suggest that north Carolina state Sen. Jim Burgin subsequently commented on the case, calling the situation “ridiculous.”.

    “Before someone evicted that lady, they should have reviewed their documents,” he told WRAL in a follow-up to the original story.

    A spokesperson for Colony Townhome Apartments told the site that the property’s owners were gathering information about the eviction and expected to provide an enhancement at a later date.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pakistan's telecommunications authority, the PTA, has confirmed that internet connectivity challenges affecting the country's residents are related to the failure of an international submarine cable. SEA-ME-WE 5 is located almost seven miles off the coast of Pakistan, near the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz, and connects the region with European networks via the Middle East. The TWA says that the outage may have caused intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality, with Transworld Associates (TWA) working to identify the cause of the issue. No timeframe has been provided for when a fix will be available yet, but for now, internet traffic has been rerouted to minimize the impact of the outage.

    In a recent development, the outage comes weeks after the Islamic Republic of Iran described several undersea fiber cables that run through the Strait of Hormuz as "legitimate new targets" in the ongoing tensions in the area. February's start of military action by the United States, Israel, and others has made the Strait of Hormuz a household name in recent months. General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, pointed out that as many as seven "large cables pass beneath the Strait of Hormuz, and all internet and commercial data pass through them," going on to say they are "legitimate" targets for the group.

    In a recent development, one of the international submarine cable systems, the SEA-ME-WE 5 (SMW5), have reported a fault at about 11 KM from Pakistan shore which may cause some internet users to experience intermittent connectivity complications and a decline in service quality. Transworld Associates (TWA) is coordinating with the SMW5 Consortium to identify the root cause of the fault and determine the Estimated Time for Restoration (ETTR). In the meantime, internet traffic is being rerouted through alternative international links to minimise the impact and ensure service continuity to the greatest extent possible. #SMW5 #SubmarineCableFault #InternetDisruption #InternetUpdate #PakistanInternet #ConnectivityUpdate #InternetServices #DigitalPakistan #PTA #TransworldAssociates #TelecomUpdate #NetworkRestoration #StayConnected #InternetConnectivityNovember 18, 2026.

    Industry observers note that notably, the SEA-ME-WE 5 cable does run through the Strait of Hormuz, although it should be stressed that there is presently no indication that this outage was caused by any act of sabotage. However, that is no doubt something that the TWA investigation will seek to confirm before it can apply whatever fix is necessary to fully restore services for those in the region.

    In a recent development, undersea cables are vital for maintaining connectivity between nations and continents, and Iran isn't the only one to have taken note. A Russian ship was chased from British waters by a Royal Navy attack helicopter earlier this year after it was found less than a mile from five undersea cables. The ship was in the area for 14 hours, and the cables it was near happened to connect the UK with Spain, Portugal, Canada, and the United States.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (675 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

    Intel 18A yields hit 70% as company signs Microsoft as EMIB customer

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, mentioned on Thursday that yields of chips made using the manufacturer's latest 18A (1.8nm-class) fabrication process have achieved 70%, which is more or less in line with what one would expect from an all-new manufacturing technology at this stage of its ramp.
    • "When I took over [as CEO in March, 2025], 18A yield was horrible; now we are at 70%," Lip-Bu Tan remarked at the TomorrowX conference (via @firesidealpha).
    • Sources indicate that lip-Bu Tan did not specify whether he meant functional yield, parametric yield, or percentage of sellable silicon.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, mentioned on Thursday that yields of chips made using the manufacturer's latest 18A (1.8nm-class) fabrication process have achieved 70%, which is more or less in line with what one would expect from an all-new manufacturing technology at this stage of its ramp. In addition, Intel and Microsoft have signed an agreement under which Microsoft will secure Intel Xeon supply capacity for years to come and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for in-house silicon.

    "When I took over [as CEO in March, 2025], 18A yield was horrible; now we are at 70%," Lip-Bu Tan remarked at the TomorrowX conference (via @firesidealpha).

    Sources indicate that lip-Bu Tan did not specify whether he meant functional yield, parametric yield, or percentage of sellable silicon. However, it is reasonable to expect a CEO of a semiconductor organization to talk about functional die yield, the percentage of dies that pass basic electrical and functional testing.

    Intel began volume production of compute tiles of its Core Ultra 300-series CPUs codenamed Panther Lake using 18A in the second half of 2025, so a 70% functional yield seems decent at this stage of the product ramp, though for Intel's economics a lot depends on parametric yield and how many advanced SKUs of Core Ultra 300-series 'Panther Lake' processors Intel can supply to customers at a premium. The same applies to Intel's Xeon 6+ Clearwater Forest processors with up to 288 cores that are in high-volume production now and which use 18A-based compute chiplets along with Foveros Direct 3D stacking.

    In addition to announcing an notable 18A milestone, Intel also signed a long-term agreement with Microsoft, under which the latter will secure multi-year Intel Xeon supply capacity, including supply of next-generation Xeon processors codenamed Diamond Rapids, and will use Intel's EMIB advanced packaging technology for multi-chiplet data center solutions developed in-house.

    The EMIB agreement is arguably the biggest news. Microsoft is the first organization to publicly commit to Intel's advanced packaging technology for its own silicon (i.e., it does not mean that Microsoft is the first third party to use EMIB; it is the first party to confirm usage of EMIB), which represents a significant commercial development for Intel Foundry in terms of publicity. However, the announcement does not identify the processors involved, their manufacturing process, production volumes, or deployment schedule. Microsoft was the first company to commit to use Intel's 18A for its data center silicon in 2024, though it is unclear whether the newly declared EMIB packaging agreement relates to the same solution or not. As the majority of high-end data center solutions tend to use multi-chiplet design, it is reasonable to expect Microsoft's future solutions for data centers to use EMIB for multi-die processors.

    "Through use of our advanced packaging capabilities with EMIB to scale future generations of Azure infrastructure, Intel and Microsoft can combine the flexibility of heterogeneous integration with the manufacturing scale required for the AI era — giving customers new levels of performance and economics when interacting with Azure," said Naga Chandrasekaran, EVP, Chief Technology and Operations Officer and General Manager of Intel Foundry.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    The Xeon agreement provides Intel with greater visibility into future server CPU demand. Importantly, Microsoft has committed to using Intel's next-generation Xeon 'Diamond Rapids,' although the announcement does not disclose purchase volumes or financial terms.

    Industry observers note that the collaboration extends beyond processor procurement and EMIB. Specifically, Intel and Microsoft are jointly developing infrastructure capabilities that encompass processor architecture, heterogeneous integration, CXL memory expansion, QuickAssist Technology (QAT) acceleration, and Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) security.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • GTA 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake are being hit with waves of zero-score user reviews on Metacritic, with fans of each game appearing to target the other.
    • The two share more than a fanbase rivalry, as GTA 6 landed a 99 Metascore at launch, tying the original 1998 Ocarina of Time for the highest critic score in the site’s history.
    • While critics have been near-unanimous in their praise, GTA 6’s user score on PlayStation 5 has fallen to 5.0, with thousands of negative ratings arriving within a day of launch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GTA 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake are being hit with waves of zero-score user reviews on Metacritic, with fans of each game appearing to target the other.

    The two share more than a fanbase rivalry, as GTA 6 landed a 99 Metascore at launch, tying the original 1998 Ocarina of Time for the highest critic score in the site’s history.

    While critics have been near-unanimous in their praise, GTA 6’s user score on PlayStation 5 has fallen to 5.0, with thousands of negative ratings arriving within a day of launch.

    That’s in stark contrast to the PlayStation Store, where ratings can only be left by players who own the game, and GTA 6 currently holds a score of 4.84 out of 5.

    Sources indicate that people like this are so lazy. Metacritic is not the only place that people can rate games. But it IS one of the most accessible (meaning it's susceptible to review bombing).PS5 players can rate the games in the Playstation store, and it's at the moment at 4.84/5. https://t.co/BBo090644U pic.twitter.com/s3X7YnbjGX.

    Some of the accounts leaving zero scores on Metacritic have barely rated anything else, with Nintendo’s Ocarina of Time remake the only other game on their profile, scored a perfect 10.

    One of those reviews blasted Rockstar for “making us wait 13 years for an 80-100$ (maybe invisible or stolen) code in a box that only runs at 30 FPS,” calling it “a buggy mess at launch.”.

    Another took aim at the game’s £100 ($132) digital-only price, adding, “This is the beginning of the end for Sony and Rockstar.”.

    The Ocarina of Time remake released on Nintendo Switch 2 on November 5, and by November 8 held a 9.6 user score, the highest in Metacritic’s history.

    According to recent reports, that has since dropped to 9.0, with a fresh batch of zero scores aimed squarely at Nintendo fans. “Fan forever GTA 6. Go cry fans of Zelda,” one read.

    Others were more direct about why they were leaving them, with one zero-score review simply reading, “Y’all losers review bombing GTA 6.”.

    GTA 6 is the joint best-reviewed game of all-time.

    Zelda Ocarina of Time remake sells 5.2 million copies in four days to break Switch 2 record.

    GTA 6 fans concerned for game following major Rockstar leak.

    It isn’t clear which side started it, with GTA 6 fans claiming Nintendo players flooded Rockstar’s game first, and some Zelda fans insisting it was the other way around.

    Not every negative GTA 6 review is part of the feud, with some players taking matter with the game’s 30fps cap on consoles, frame rate drops, and open-world bugs.

    Others have objected to the game’s optional romance system and claimed GTA 6 has gone “woke,” while some simply called it “the biggest disappointment in gaming history.”.

    Unlike the PlayStation Store, Metacritic doesn’t require owners to prove they own a game before leaving a rating.

    #70069. Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1471 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

    Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.
    • Sources indicate that I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy.
    • The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that crucial to me day-to-day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

    Sources indicate that I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

    The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that crucial to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

    Recent findings suggest that the design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

    My love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

    After a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

    Recent findings suggest that despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

    In a recent development, if you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

    Tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

    It has been revealed that I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

    Sources indicate that we could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

    I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the new connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this glitch.

    This is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

    Sources indicate that when the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

    In a recent development, swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That noted, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

    It has been revealed that I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”.

    In a recent development, with audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

    This had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

    One of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an patch, so here’s hoping.

    Sources indicate that I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

    It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

    According to recent reports, the experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

    Coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the new “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

    According to recent reports, there is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, there’s a new vibe-coded OS in town going by the name of LiberNT.
    • According to recent reports, liberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a significant leap.
    • It has been revealed that this still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, there’s a new vibe-coded OS in town going by the name of LiberNT. Its name provides a big clue to its nature: Liber (free), NT (New Technology architecture, as in Windows NT). As it has been released under GNU’s GPL3.0 license, LiberNT also provides a free new way to run apps designed for Microsoft’s Windows 11.

    According to recent reports, liberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a significant leap. Reading the intro, you might have wondered if this work had a ReactOS connection, and indeed there is. But what started as a fork of ReactOS has already got a upcoming boot loader, graphics stack, memory manager – and yesterday a new kernel. “LiberNT is not affiliated with or endorsed by the ReactOS project or Microsoft,” insist the devs behind this OS.

    It has been revealed that this still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64. Ambitiously, the goal is to develop this OS to deliver a free Windows alternative that is “stable, reliable and efficient.” On that latter point, yesterday’s blog upgrade relays some impressive efficiency and performance stats.

    Industry observers note that the LiberNT team has benchmarked their eponymous OS against Microsoft’s Windows NT, and it beats it hands-down in 112 of 132 system tests. The testing assessed performance in the following areas: file caching, memory handling, threads and locks, plus FAT32 and NTFS storage. Interestingly, both the free and commercial OS were benchmarked on a Mac with an Apple M3 Pro chip. We scanned through the results, and the worst loss for LiberNT was a 28% performance deficit vs Win11, but it claims some astounding relative performance wins showing the free OS being over 2000% faster.

    Industry observers note that the devs are entirely clear about the fact that the operating system was vibe coded. “AI is part of how LiberNT is built. It helps us review and write code, and everything it writes is then reviewed by a human,” explains a section of the GitHub page for the project. “Before anything reaches the main branch, a person runs and validates the end-to-end tests. We care about this project too much to let a regression slip through.”.

    Industry observers note that if the above highlights about this fresh OS's scope, mission, compatibility, and performance have whetted your appetite, there is the full code available via the GitHub link (top), and even some ready-made builds as bootable disk images. Indeed, I’m quite eager to give this new OS a spin. Hopefully, it works as well as the ambitious developers suggest, and I won’t be disappointed by any stability concerns using my daily productivity apps like Firefox, Word, and an old release of Photoshop.

    Vivo X500 Pro camera review: Battle of the small(er) phones vs Pixel 11 Pro

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?
    • According to recent reports, over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company.
    • It has been revealed that the answer is mostly yes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?

    According to recent reports, over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company. The first time I used a Vivo X100 Pro blew my mind in a way smartphone cameras hadn’t for a few years, but does the company’s 4th iteration — yes, Vivo skipped the X400 — of the X series still impress?

    It has been revealed that the answer is mostly yes. The Vivo X500 series includes five models: the base X500, the X500 Pro, and the X500 Pro Max. Unlike some other phones, all three of these models feature different camera hardware that takes advantage of the physical size differences. The X500 Pro Max’s hardware is the best of the bunch, but that phone is substantially larger and heavier as a result.

    So I’m comparing the more reasonably sized models to see which semi-compact Vivo phone you should consider this year. I tossed the Google Pixel 11 Pro into the comparison since Google also offers a compact flagship camera phone.

    Most camera specs between these phones are surprisingly comparable, so the differences you’re about to see are largely caused by some pretty massive differences in processing. I already covered Vivo’s wild fresh AI camera mode, so let’s go for something a little closer to normal smartphone camera use: a day at the Biltmore.

    Perhaps the biggest difference between these phones is Vivo’s pursuit of “perfection,” while Google seems to embrace a more “natural” look. At 10x and 5x, the photos from both Vivo phones are essentially noise-free, have clear sharpening applied to them, and are generally quite vibrant. Despite having similar specs, the Vivo X500 Pro’s more advanced Sony LYT telephoto sensor pulls out more detail.

    Google’s images are notably softer, although not in a low-resolution sort of way. They look more like they’re taken from a standard camera rather than a smartphone, which some people may prefer. While telephoto image quality between the Vivo X500 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro is mostly down to preference, Google’s phone is substantially faster while taking the actual photo. In all of the darker shots, the Pixel 11 Pro took the picture instantly. Both Vivo X500 models took a 2-3 second exposure shot, making me stand there for longer than I’m used to.

    It has been revealed that ultrawide performance is where I feel we see the largest gap between these phones. Both the Vivo X500 and X500 Pro cameras offer bright, well-balanced shots that are vibrant but not unrealistic. The light sources in the room emit a lovely warm glow, yet the bulbs themselves aren’t overblown. The X500 Pro’s slightly warmer image across all three scenarios looks best to me.

    Industry observers note that the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide images are often underexposed and lacking in dynamic range. The staircase shot exhibits this problem the most. This can come off as natural in some scenarios, as modern smartphone photography is notorious for brightening dark areas too much, but too often the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide shots just feel unnaturally dark.

    Recent findings suggest that the main camera is much more balanced, although it’s fun to push these phones to find their weaknesses. One of the best examples of differing priorities is in the wreath shot, which was quite dark in real life thanks to the bright sunlight outside. The Pixel 11 Pro valiantly tried to brighten up the shadows so you could actually see the wreath (since it’s clearly the subject), causing the rest of the scene to look forcefully bright.

    The same glitch cropped up in the image of the wine rack, where both Vivo phones captured a nicer-looking shot. The image of the trellis walkway is a tie, but the photo of my ridiculous bowl of ice cream looks best on the Vivo X500 Pro, once again.

    In a recent development, portrait mode is where I think the Vivo X500 Pro is the clear loser, but it’s not for any of the reasons in the other categories above. Rather, the X500 Pro seems to have some weird warping happening in the bokeh processing that’s not present on the base Vivo X500. This is in both front-facing and rear camera portrait shots, so it’s not a lens issue or some weird setting.

    Google cleaned up its portrait shots so much this year that it’s borderline ridiculous. Pixels had the worst portrait mode for years, but this year’s overhaul of the portrait algorithm made all the difference in the world.

    Overall, the Vivo X500 series is another solid release for Vivo, and while neither the base nor Pro models offer the same top-tier camera specs as the Pro Max model, it’s clear Vivo pulled off something great. The Vivo X500 Pro retails for €1,399 in the EU, while the base X500 global model is a little harder to find, but should be quite a bit cheaper if you can get your hands on it.

    More information about the alleged knowledge of chip diversion by a Supermicro executive is being revealed as shareholders’ civil lawsuit against the organization progresses. According to The Telegraph, the investors alleged that there was “no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge about the company’s illicit sales.” Chen, the former Chief Growth Officer at Supermicro and described by a colleague as the company’s sales leader, resigned from her position in April of this year — about a month after the three Supermicro employees, including its co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, were arrested for a $2.5-billion AI GPU smuggling scheme.

    It has been revealed that cenly Chen is married to former Nvidia Executive Vice President of Worldwide Field Operations Jay Puri, who is also described as the manufacturer’s sales chief. The Information also called him Jensen Huang’s right-hand man and stated he was the person that Nvidia’s customers turned to if they wanted to buy chips or had other pressing concerns. The shareholders’ accusations and her relationship with Puri have put the former Supermicro executive in the spotlight, especially after Huang’s sudden departure from the AI chipmaker amid a flurry of affairs and smuggling accusations.

    Sources say that Puri controlled the AI chip allocations to server manufacturers, including Supermicro, while the lawsuit claims that Chen decided how many Nvidia racks each Supermicro customer could get. A former Supermicro employee was also quoted in the complaint saying that it was “widely known within the Organization that Chen had to leave because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips with serial numbers associated with the GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China.” This apparently refers to the serial numbers that were moved from real to dummy servers using a hairdryer.

    In a recent development, supermicro has noted multiple times that it has cooperated with the U.S. government regarding the smuggling investigation and that it has not been included in the lawsuit against the three defendants. Furthermore, the organization has denied her involvement regarding Nvidia GPU allocations. “Chen did not manage Supermicro’s relationship with Nvidia and did not decide how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers,” a Supermicro spokesperson told The Information. They also said that she left voluntarily and that her LinkedIn profile now reads her current position as CEO of ChronoScale, an Nvidia cloud partner based in Silicon Valley. As for Puri, he stepped away from his position at Nvidia in late August, about two months before the Jensen Huang scandal blew up, although he remains as an advisor to the AI chipmaker.

    Google Play wants Android apps to nail foldable basics by April 2027

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (331 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google Play is introducing latest adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.
    • Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables.
    • It has been revealed that referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Play is introducing latest adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.

    Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables.

    It has been revealed that referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen. During rotation, resizing, and folding/unfolding, apps must preserve scroll position, text input, and media playback. Apps must also support multi-window environments.

    Apps that do not meet this quality bar will no longer be able to publish or update on Google Play, and may have reduced visibility on the store.

    At the same time, Google Play will require foldable device screenshots for app listings: “Providing foldable screenshots by April 2027 will become a standard submission requirement when publishing latest apps or updating your store listing.”.

    Curious to see whether the requirements will actually be as strict as they make them seem (on paper).

    If so, then also Google will have a ton of work to do to modernise all of their apps.

    By August 2027, new and updated apps will be required to target Android 17 (API level 37).

    Over time, this “quality framework will progressively expand to incorporate Tier 2 and Tier 1 standards across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, and Android XR.”.

    Apps that meet Tier 2 (better) or Tier 1 (best) will get “premier store badging, editorial spotlighting, and enhanced merchandising across Google Play as the platform bar elevates.”.

    On the gaming front, titles will need to add foldable screenshots to listings by April 2027, while Tier 3 large screen quality guidelines go into effect in August 2027.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A streamer’s PS5 began smoking while they were away for a toilet break mid-way through their play through of GTA 6.

    GTA 6 finally rolled out on November 19, following years of anticipation, with millions of players diving into Rockstar’s latest open-world blockbuster.

    However, the launch hasn’t been entirely smooth, with PS5 and Xbox players reporting game-breaking crashes. Some have encountered recurring errors that prevent them from progressing, while others have been unable to get past the opening minutes of the game.

    On November 21, Twitch streamer JoJoJosiah took to X to share news that their PS5 had begun smoking during a GTA 6 livestream, apparently leaving the console unusable.

    It has been revealed that “Was playing GTA VI on stream but had to go poop,” they explained. “Paused it and put on a sensory vid for my chat.”.

    However, while they were away, the streamer claimed their “PS5 started just smoking out its a**.” The post was accompanied by a video of the incident.

    In the video, JoJoJosiah arrives back at their streaming setup to find the room filled with smoke, while they panic and figure out what to do, before the fire alarm goes off.

    Was playing gta VI on stream but had to go poop. Paused it and put on a sensory vid for my chatPS5 started just smoking out its ass and now i need to get a replacement 😀 pic.twitter.com/qSdfcCi4l1.

    In a recent development, in a reply to the original tweet, the streamer noted that they were uninjured as a result of the fire. “I’m fine and everything is good tho,” they wrote.

    It’s still unclear what caused the console to malfunction, or whether GTA 6 itself played any role in the reported hardware failure, but the streamer revealed that they now need to purchase a replacement console as a result.

    Latest Update: Intel continues layoffs with cuts to its IT department, hundreds of employees reportedly affected

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the tech giant's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough.
    • In a recent development, the latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech.
    • The latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the tech giant's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough. The company has reportedly initiated another round of layoffs, this time across its global information technology (IT) organization, as its chief executive continues to reduce expenses and simplify the company's operations, reports Business Insider.

    In a recent development, the latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech. Some employees claim that the reductions could affect a double-digit percentage of the department's workforce of around 2,607 people at 55 sites in 53 countries, so we are talking about at least 260 people if we are talking about a 10% reduction, or as much as 520 if we are talking about a 20% reduction. One has to keep in mind that these estimates have not been independently verified. Intel has neither confirmed the number of affected employees nor identified the specific teams involved. Instead, the tech giant reiterated to Business Insider that it regularly reviews its workforce to ensure that personnel and financial resources correspond to its strategic priorities.

    The latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026. In July, Intel eliminated positions in its Data Center and AI Group. Between July and October, the company submitted nine Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) notices in California, which covered 222 employees, according to Business Insider. The most recent notice, filed on October 22, concerned 67 permanent job cuts at Intel's Folsom campus (which mostly specializes in R&D, hardware validation, and software development), effective October 31. As of November 17, no additional WARN notices had been reported.

    Intel employed 81,100 people as of September 27, 2026, including 76,500 employees at Intel itself and another 4,600 at Mobileye and other subsidiaries. This compares with 85,100 employees at the end of 2025 and 108,900 a year earlier, which means that the company's workforce declined by 4,000 since December, 2025, and 27,800 since December, 2024. respectively.

    Industry observers note that intel's workforce reductions began well before Lip-Bu Tan became chief executive in 2025. In 2024, his predecessor Pat Gelsinger announced plans to eliminate more than 15,000 positions, or approximately 15% of the tech giant’s workforce. Tan has continued to reduce expenses, eliminate management layers, and discontinue lower-priority projects as Intel attempts to cut costs and reduce losses/improve profitability.

    A Louisiana coffee shop co-owner claims she refused to serve a TikTok creator who returned to her Baton Rouge cafe after posting two negative reviews.

    Sources indicate that victoria Arroyo co-owns Pura Vida Coffee Bar, a cafe near Louisiana State University. TikTok creator Fabian Beaucoudray had criticized the shop’s coffee and food in earlier videos, and Arroyo included clips from those reviews in her response.

    Recent findings suggest that in one review she also posted to Snapchat, Beaucoudray said she went back to give the cafe a second chance. She took issue with paying $3 for what she described as five small pieces of potato alongside a $10 sandwich.

    Beaucoudray posted about being refused service on November 19. She had returned to the cafe with a friend, according to a recap from TikTok creator thenameisblossom. Beaucoudray wrote in the caption of her own video that she had “never seen a company take a bad review this serious.”.

    Sources indicate that arroyo said she was working the register when she recognized Beaucoudray and decided to turn her away. According to Arroyo, Beaucoudray had left both times without mentioning her complaints to staff. Arroyo said that she left the shop without a chance to address the problems before the videos went up.

    Arroyo tagged Beaucoudray in her November 20 response and addressed her directly in the caption. “I am genuinely sorry if you were embarrassed today, that was never my intention,” she wrote.

    Arroyo’s response passed one million views, while some commenters defended her decision, and others noted the videos made them want to visit the shop.
