    #70028. What if Vampire Survivors met Grand Theft Auto 2? Maniac is a brilliant mash-up that dares to ask that question

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (946 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

    What if Vampire Survivors met Grand Theft Auto 2? Maniac is a brilliant mash-up that dares to ask that question

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that what would you get if you combined the chaotic top-down action of old-school Grand Theft Auto 2 with the chaotic top-down action of Vampire Survivors?
    • Recent findings suggest that your goal is simple: survive for as long as you can or until the 20-minute clock hits zero.
    • Industry observers note that maniac's debt to GTA is clear, and its chaotic action is brilliantly realised as it channels the compelling rhythms of a Survivors-style roguelite, where randomness in items and level layout makes each run fresh as you strive to unlock new characters, progressing a little further each time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that what would you get if you combined the chaotic top-down action of old-school Grand Theft Auto 2 with the chaotic top-down action of Vampire Survivors? That's the question Soldat and King Arthur's Gold developer Transhuman asked when it started working on 2024's roguelite shooter Maniac. The result is a delight, yet Maniac remains frustratingly underappreciated.

    Recent findings suggest that your goal is simple: survive for as long as you can or until the 20-minute clock hits zero. Throughout that time, your secondary objective is to create as much mayhem as possible - painting the road with the blood of your foes, slamming cars into buildings, performing drive-bys as you rampage across the procedurally-generated city. The more carnage you cause, the higher your Wanted level, until you're fending off police and the military.

    Industry observers note that maniac's debt to GTA is clear, and its chaotic action is brilliantly realised as it channels the compelling rhythms of a Survivors-style roguelite, where randomness in items and level layout makes each run fresh as you strive to unlock new characters, progressing a little further each time. It's a relatively slight experience, as its £4 price tag reflects, featuring a single compact map, just six characters, and barely any permanent progression. But Maniac makes a spirited argument for a return to a simpler time when GTA was all about shooting cops, stealing cars, and indiscriminately murdering pedestrians rather than the 'everything' game it is today.

    Recent findings suggest that maniac is also a game that feels like it's trying to make good on an idea many of us had when we first played GTA 1 & 2 all those years ago: what would a better-looking, more advanced version of that look like? And for developer Michał Marcinkowski, Maniac's genesis also harkens back to an earlier time. "When I was 12, I used to come back from school and play the demo of GTA 1," he tells me over email. "It was top-down and time-limited, and all I'd do was try to cause as much chaos as possible within the 20 minutes of the demo.".

    And there's perhaps a hint of a 12-year-old's exuberance to Maniac. There's the bright colour palette and gleeful chaos of its physics-driven mechanics, the adrenaline rush its aggressive enemy AI creates, and its absurd roster of playable characters, which range from Little Girl to Hotdog Guy. "Each [character] is a bit of me and a bit of you," Marcinkowski explains. "We all have a drunk Santa in us. We all have a pathetic hot-dog-suit guy inside of us. Each character failed at something and is lashing out.".

    As each new Grand Theft Auto game pushes further into realism, the idea of recreating the rampages seen in classic GTA feels increasingly unpalatable, but Maniac's colourful cartoon aesthetic means it can get away with more. One Achievement, with a flourish of old-school bad-taste humour, challenges players to destroy five school buses using an airstrike ability called Santa's Little Helpers. And that level of irreverent, chaotic lunacy escalates the deeper into each session you get, particularly as your Wanted level climbs: if you antagonise law enforcement enough here, they eventually break out a game-ending nuke.

    "This comes back to being 12," Marcinkowski says. "Nukes are just cool. I wanted the game to end with a bang, and what's more maniacal and exaggerated than a nuke? So that idea was with me for more than 20 years.".

    Recent findings suggest that core to Maniac's design is the ability to change from a Survivors-like auto-shooter to a standard shooter where you're able to control your aim. The latter option is, I think, the more fitting one, particularly given how much driving you do. If you squint, it almost feels like a GTA 2 clone. And while the Vampire Survivors inspirations are plentiful - including its now-standard three-option upgrade system - the GTA elements are clearly the more prevalent.

    According to recent reports, it might not play exactly like a GTA game, but it certainly captures the series' early days spirit. And Marcinkowski states he's surprised more developers haven't tried to riff on GTA: "You'd expect the most popular game in the world to have hundreds of clones, but that's not the case." There may be a reason for that.

    It has been revealed that as major as modern-day GTA is, clones are apparently much less popular. "When you look at the sales data, particularly of top-down GTA clones, they don't sell well", explains Marcinkowski. "I found that out way too late, and I thought Maniac wouldn't be a hit." His publisher was initially equally buoyant too. "But then they studied the market and stopped being so hyped. That's how it felt as we got close to release. The wishlist count wasn't very high.".

    Sources indicate that "I was expecting 10,000 [copies sold]," Marcinkowski tells me. "I actually started making another game two months before Maniac came out because I thought I'd go broke." But then the game launched, and early worries proved unfounded. It sold more than 100K copies, comfortably blowing past its maker's modest expectations, putting it in the top one percent of games released on Steam.

    It's a surprise success story built on the foundations of Marcinkowski's youth, and as we chat about GTA, he reveals he's less keen on Rockstar's modern games, which lack that classic gameplay drive. "I always liked the counter-culture side of GTA, which is why I put so much of it into Maniac," he elaborates. "GTA 6 seems to have become pop culture, so it's lost its appeal for me." Marcinkowski's heart, it seems, is old-school.

That drive can hit reads and writes of 7,940 and 6,900 MB/s, compared to the 14,800 MB/s and 13,400 MB/s here. Even slower speeds are managed with a Gen 3 SSD, and below 600 MB/s with an older-style SATA drive.

    It has been revealed that you aren't getting the fastest Gen 5 drive here, but that's not really the point. You're getting a high-performance drive with a decent amount of capacity that, with this discount, you're going to struggle to beat when you compare cost to performance.

    Recent findings suggest that at $0.174 per GB, this 2TB Samsung 9100 Pro for $349.99 is one of the best value options for a new gaming PC build or upgrade if you need storage. We'd expect this Amazon Black Friday deal to be very popular, so if you want to grab this top Samsung drive at a discount, you'd better be quick.

    #70022. Power and cooling limits force AI clusters with 100,000+ accelerators to use multiple data centers

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (957 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

    Power and cooling limits force AI clusters with 100,000+ accelerators to use multiple data centers

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The rapid growth of AI clusters is pushing computing infrastructure beyond the physical and power limitations of individual data centers, which creates demand for newly introduced networking architectures capable of connecting compute resources across multiple facilities and even geographical regions.
    • In a recent development, modern AI clusters typically accommodate more than 100,000 AI accelerators and potentially millions of CPU endpoints, placing tremendous demands on network bandwidth, latency, and congestion management.
    • Industry observers note that traditionally, high-performance computing systems have relied on two major interconnect domains: scale-up and scale-out.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The rapid growth of AI clusters is pushing computing infrastructure beyond the physical and power limitations of individual data centers, which creates demand for newly introduced networking architectures capable of connecting compute resources across multiple facilities and even geographical regions. At Supercomputing 2026 (SC26), researchers from The Ohio State University discussed the evolution of high-performance networking technologies. At the conference, they explained how efficient distributed computing at such a scale requires considerably more than faster network connections, highlighting the importance of scale across domains to stretch workloads across different data centers in separate geographical regions.

    In a recent development, modern AI clusters typically accommodate more than 100,000 AI accelerators and potentially millions of CPU endpoints, placing tremendous demands on network bandwidth, latency, and congestion management. Meanwhile, an accelerator's computational performance continues to increase faster than communication capabilities, which means that faster AI GPUs do not necessarily deliver proportional improvements in application performance. As a result, the efficiency of network infrastructure determines how effectively large-scale AI systems can use their computational resources.

    Industry observers note that traditionally, high-performance computing systems have relied on two major interconnect domains: scale-up and scale-out. Scale-up networks connect processors and accelerators within tightly integrated systems using technologies like AMD's Infinity Fabric, Intel's UPI, Nvidia's NVLink, or emerging alternatives such as UALink. Scale-out networks, which typically rely on Ethernet, InfiniBand, HPE Slingshot, or, more recently, Ultra Ethernet, connect individual servers or rack-scale systems into larger clusters. These interconnects have different requirements for bandwidth, latency, and scalability, which is why they serve different purposes.

    It has been revealed that however, the massive size and power consumption of modern AI clusters create demand for a third interconnect domain, known as scale-across. Unlike scale-out networks, which typically connect systems within a single data center, scale-across architectures extend high-performance connectivity between different buildings, campuses, or even regions.

    Such an approach enables operators to combine computational and other resources from multiple locations to achieve a certain level of performance rather than to bring an excessive number of accelerators to a single data center, which may be hard, or even impossible, due to power availability, cooling requirements, or physical space constraints.

    The transition toward scale-across architectures has already begun. Google introduced its Virgo network architecture earlier this year to support AI workloads that exceed the space and power capacity of individual data centers. The firm intends to treat an entire campus of computing facilities as a single system, albeit with specialized networks for communication between accelerators, servers, and data centers. Cisco and Marvell are also developing technologies for scale-across deployments, including high-capacity routers, switching chips, and optical interconnects designed to connect geographically distributed clusters.

    Sources indicate that extending AI infrastructure beyond individual facilities introduces substantial technical challenges. While modern scale-up networks offer extremely high bandwidth and low latency over relatively short distances, communication between data centers must contend with the physical limitations of long-distance connections. Even optical networks cannot eliminate propagation delays, whereas congestion, packet loss, and synchronization overhead can further reduce effective performance. Consequently, connecting two large GPU clusters with high-speed links does not necessarily make them behave like one tightly integrated computing system.

    According to recent reports, these challenges are particularly notable for AI training, where accelerators frequently exchange model parameters, gradients, and intermediate results. Large-scale workloads require efficient collective communications, as delays that affect individual accelerators dramatically reduce the performance of the entire cluster. Therefore, the efficiency of distributed computing depends not only on raw network bandwidth, but also on network topology, congestion management, communication protocols, and software implementations.

    It has been revealed that to address these limitations, network adapters and switches are becoming more sophisticated than ever. Modern network interface controllers can perform Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) operations without continuous CPU involvement, whereas technologies such as HPE Slingshot hardware collectives and Nvidia SHARP can offload certain communication operations to the network infrastructure itself. SmartNICs and data processing units further reduce the burden on host processors as they handle selected network and infrastructure functions in dedicated hardware. Such capabilities can improve efficiency of distributed applications without necessarily requiring faster physical interconnects.

    Sources indicate that interestingly, software plays an equally important role in the performance of large-scale AI infrastructure, as communication frameworks like libfabric, MPI, or UCX determine how applications exchange data and use the capabilities of modern network adapters. Also, GPU-aware communication and technologies like GPUDirect RDMA can eliminate unnecessary transfers through host memory, while optimized collective operations can reduce communication overhead across large numbers of accelerators, according to the researchers.

    The growing complexity of AI infrastructure also changes how operators should evaluate network performance. Although the industry continues to introduce faster interconnect technologies, including versions of GbE with nominal bandwidths of 800 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s, peak transfer rates alone do not fully describe the capabilities of a given system because the performance of actual applications depends on multiple factors, including how effectively network hardware and software cooperate to transfer data, prevent congestion, and synchronize computations across thousands of processors.

    Ultimately, the emergence of scale-across interconnection architectures reflects a fundamental change in the design of AI infrastructure. As the computational capabilities of individual accelerators increase and AI clusters expand beyond individual facilities, efficient communication becomes just as key as processor performance. As a result, the next generation of AI systems will depend not only on faster AI accelerators or CPUs, but also on sophisticated network adapters, switches, and, perhaps more importantly, software that can unite geographically distributed computational resources without excessive communication overhead.

    Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

This is the lowest-ever price that this particular laptop has been listed on Amazon, and a $575 saving from its all-time high $1,754.99 listing price; it's also a handy saving on the typical price of $1,586, which Amazon has recorded over the last 90 days. This is a good price for a budget gaming laptop if you want to get into some PC gaming for the first time, or just be able to play PC games whilst away from your main gaming rig.

The rest of the laptop is nearly identical, though. We really liked the solid performance for the value, but found the speakers in the system a little lacklustre.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign.
    • Previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar.
    • The tabs remain Home, Blueprint, Billing, Shop, and Support.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign.

    Previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar. With the network switching enhancement announced last week, Google Fi now has a floating navigation toolbar.

    The tabs remain Home, Blueprint, Billing, Shop, and Support. A pill-shaped tab indicator is leveraged, while there’s a prominent shadow effect. Given the floating nature, you see what’s around the toolbar, while Fi Wireless now extends underneath the system navigation bar.

    However, the Shop tab loads a webpage as before, resulting in a gap and wasted space.

    Sources indicate that there’s now a floating action button for the new Google AI-powered Ask Fi chatbot. It provides “instant account help and troubleshooting.” If you ask for human support, the contents of the conversation carry over.

    It has been revealed that this redesign is rolling out with version 171 of the app as a server-side upgrade. Google Fi joins Google Photos, Chat, and Pixel Now Playing in adopting floating navigation, which is likely the fresh first-party mandate for a more edge-to-edge design.

    Recent findings suggest that secondary network switching is not yet widely available, with Google telling us last week that it’s a gradual rollout. The MVNO is also ending Pixel exclusivity for Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ with availability on “select” Samsung and Motorola phones.

    #70015. MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ review: RTX Spark power comes to Windows on Arm desktops, but there are trade-offs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3372 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

    MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ review: RTX Spark power comes to Windows on Arm desktops, but there are trade-offs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, MSI's EdgeMesa N AI+ mini PC brings Nvidia RTX Spark power to a Windows on Arm desktop.
    • Solid local AI performance for LLMs and image generation, as expected.
    • Familiar Windows 11 user experience and app compatibility.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, MSI's EdgeMesa N AI+ mini PC brings Nvidia RTX Spark power to a Windows on Arm desktop. It offers broad app compatibility and the same strong local AI performance we've come to expect from Nvidia's GB10 SoC, but it's still very expensive and less expandable than DGX Spark systems.

    Solid local AI performance for LLMs and image generation, as expected.

    Familiar Windows 11 user experience and app compatibility.

    Could use more peripheral I/O and smarter port placement.

    Loses the DGX Spark's clustering capability.

    Getting the best gaming performance requires patience.

    Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

    In a recent development, nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, powered by the RTX Spark N1X SoC, passed its most difficult test yet last month at the heart of Windows on Arm laptops. Now we get to see how that chip serves as a Windows on Arm foundation for compact desktops.

    We’ve got our hands on the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+, a $7,500 RTX Spark mini PC that gives Windows-native creators and local AI trailblazers access to the same powerful 6144-core Blackwell GPU and 20-core Arm CPU that we recently put to the test in the Surface Laptop Ultra, along with a 128GB pool of unified memory and 4TB of storage in our tested config.

    According to recent reports, we’ve been testing Nvidia GB10-powered desktop systems for almost a year now in the form of the DGX Spark and friends, and the EdgeMesa N AI+’s design is typical of the breed. It’s wrapped in a slightly hollow-feeling matte aluminum shell with shiny diamond-cut edges and a white plastic back plate.

    It has been revealed that the design and build quality of this system is a tad underwhelming for the price. It feels nice enough, but It’s hardly a precision-milled statement piece for your desk like a Mac Mini or Mac Studio.

    Industry observers note that the EdgeMesa draws cool air in through its perforated front panel, which then passes through a dual-fan heatsink with a vapor-chamber base and exhausts through the back panel. The rounded rectangle on the top half of the front panel might look like an optical drive tray, but it’s a purely cosmetic accent.

    Around back, the EdgeMesa comes equipped with a 10 Gigabit Ethernet jack, an HDMI 2.1 port, and three USB Type-C 20 Gbps ports with DisplayPort Alt Mode support. A fourth USB-C port is dedicated to the system’s 240 W USB-PD power adapter. The EdgeMesa also has Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 radios inside.

    Even with a wireless keyboard and mouse, three 20Gbps USB-C ports feel a bit skimpy as the sole expansion options on a $7,499 PC that’s positioned as a do-it-all desktop for content creation and gaming. If you need to connect multiple monitors to an RTX Spark via USB-C, those scant options for peripheral connectivity shrink even further.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    For comparison, a similarly priced Mac Studio gives you four 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5 ports around back and two more USB Type-C ports, plus an SD card reader, up front. The Mac even provides a headphone jack, while the EdgeMesa requires you to plug in a USB headset or DAC or pair Bluetooth earbuds for audio output.

    Even the Mac Mini gives you three Thunderbolt ports out back and two USB 3 10Gbps ports out front.

    According to recent reports, in use, the tightly spaced, rear-mounted USB-C ports make for an annoying time when doing frequent unplugging and replugging of devices like card readers and external SSDs that are typical in creative workflows. Even one front-panel USB-C port would have made a huge difference in the ease of use of this design.

    It has been revealed that the EdgeMesa also drops the handy ConnectX RDMA NIC that lets you cluster DGX Spark systems together to run larger AI models. That omission raises a weighty question: is Windows support and application compatibility important enough to trade away any chance of expanding your local AI foundation in the future?

    Having tested DGX Sparks for some time now, I’m not sure that’s a wise trade-off, given that most anybody reading this already has a capable Windows PC or Mac that can link up with a DGX Spark for many local AI compute jobs using the Nvidia Sync app.

    DGX Spark prices are rising, but you can get MSI's own EdgeXpert with 128GB of memory and a 4TB SSD on sale for $8,099 right now (or $8,499 at full price). Even a $1000 difference in price for that ConnectX NIC in this rarefied air of PC pricing would give me pause if I'm seriously considering how to add local AI capacity to my home.

    Recent findings suggest that if you have no inclination whatsoever to learn Linux or networking concepts and just want a no-questions-asked, AI-capable Windows mini PC that can serve as your primary desktop, an RTX Spark system like this may be the way to go. But you'll want to be really sure of your decision before dropping this much cash.

    20-core Arm CPU (10 X925 performance cores, 10 A725 efficiency cores).

    6144-core (48 SM) Nvidia Blackwell integrated GPU.

    128GB LPDDR5X, 273 GB/s shared memory bandwidth.

    10 Gigabit Ethernet, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4.

    3x USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 Type-C ports (rear).

    Industry observers note that the performance of the Nvidia GB10 SoC's CPU and GPU resources, whether under DGX OS or Windows, is well-trodden ground by this point. But for a fresh point of comparison, we grabbed AMD’s Ryzen AI Halo, swapped in a spare SSD, and installed Windows 11 Pro, as the Ryzen AI Halo is the only other Windows-ready platform with a large unified memory pool for AI adventurers.

    According to recent reports, in the Geekbench 7 CPU benchmark under Windows, the Ryzen AI Halo delivers a slightly higher single-threaded score than the MSI EdgeMesa’s RTX Spark Superchip, but its multithreaded score trails the Nvidia part. Using Linux, we would expect both scores to be higher for the Ryzen CPU. But the broader point remains the same: you can expect similar performance from both of these CPUs under Windows.

    In a recent development, we’ve left Apple’s Mac Studio with M4 Max in these charts just to emphasize the large performance lead Apple Silicon holds in this benchmark, even with older chips. The current M5 Max would likely open an even larger lead.

    In the AgentPerf-Local AI inference benchmark, the MSI EdgeMesa delivered performance practically identical to Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra when running the same Qwen 3.8 27B model with DFlash2 speculative decoding. Its desktop form factor doesn’t seem to give it any extra performance headroom, at least for this LLM serving configuration. Other workloads or models could reveal a difference.

    We already tested the RTX Spark against the Ryzen AI Halo in AgentPerf-Local in our Surface Laptop Ultra review, and AMD’s platform ended up way behind GB10 in those tests. And in this fresh round of testing, AMD's LLM performance is worse under Windows with the Vulkan backend than in Linux with ROCm, taking a whopping four times as long as the EdgeMesa to complete the benchmark.

    Strix Halo might have been an appealing local inference option when it was the only open and relatively hackable unified memory platform around, but if you’re serious about local AI performance (and especially if tokens equal dollars for you), a GB10 system is the superior choice in late 2026.

    Gaming on RTX Spark continues to be a bit of a weird time, and the MSI EdgeMesa N doesn’t change that experience, even with a more generous power and thermal budget than the Surface Laptop Ultra I've already tested.

    This platform just doesn’t respond to tuning as we might expect from our experience with traditional gaming PCs and laptops. That weirdness stems, in part, from the imbalance between memory bandwidth and compute resources on GB10.

    According to recent reports, the 48 SMs of the RTX Spark N1X GPU have to share just 273 GB/s of LPDDR5X bandwidth with the CPU. Compare that with the 672 GB/s of dedicated bandwidth the similarly-specced RTX 5070 enjoys from its 12 GB of GDDR7.

    Sources indicate that architectural decisions aside, the RTX Spark platform's gaming performance isn't helped by the fact that full GPU utilization is seemingly hampered by the overhead of Prism x86 emulation in most games. Few (if any) major titles have Arm ports, so this is just a fact of life for the foreseeable future if you buy one of these systems.

    Let's see how this all plays out in practice for the RTX Spark versus the Radeon 8060S on board AMD's Strix Halo.

    It has been revealed that in the 3DMark Steel Nomad raster benchmark, the RTX Spark holds a wide lead over the Ryzen AI Halo, delivering a roughly 56% higher score. That result would suggest a knockout in games for Nvidia’s platform.

    But Steel Nomad isn’t representative of real-world gaming performance on the RTX Spark. If we fire up Control Resonant on both platforms and choose the High raster preset at 1440p with Performance upscaling (a 1280x720 input resolution), the RTX Spark and Strix Halo end up a lot closer.

    Recent findings suggest that notably, though, the RTX Spark desktop delivers considerably worse 1% low FPS performance than the Ryzen AI Halo, and this does manifest as visible stutter and hitching. So it's not a clear win for the Nvidia platform.

    AMD fans might take heart in the fact that Strix Halo can get this close to the RTX Spark on this raster gaming baseline, but the Radeon 8060S doesn’t have nearly as many tricks up its sleeve to further juice performance.

    For one, the quality of FSR 4 upscaling at lower input resolutions on RDNA 3.5 is still not up to par with what you can get out of DLSS 4.5. For two, the Radeon 8060S’s RDNA 3.5 CUs don't match up well against the Spark's Blackwell-powered RT chops.

    And FSR Frame Generation is still limited to a doubling of a base frame rate, so you can’t smooth out gameplay on a high-refresh-rate monitor nearly as well as you can with DLSS MFG.

    So even if their raster baseline frame rates are similar, the Radeon 8060S isn't delivering the same image quality in Control Resonant as an RTX Spark system does with all its DLSS features in play.

    Sources indicate that RT is the next step for squeezing better image quality out of Control Resonant. Surprisingly, enabling RT Medium only results in a 14% performance hit on the Spark versus 38% on the AI Halo. That might be due in part to the efficiency of DLSS Ray Reconstruction versus the Northlight engine's built-in denoiser, but the RT prowess of Blackwell certainly can't hurt.

    A 52.3 FPS average with a 75 ms average PC latency is an OK baseline — at least in the context of an RTX Spark system — for adding MFG to the mix for a smoother experience, especially since Control Resonant seems to link Nvidia Reflex latency reduction to that tech anyway. But dialing in MFG 3X with the default MFG Preset B model still results in a PC latency of 96 ms on average, which is too high to be enjoyable, even if we give the Spark some slack.

    I found that the fresh MFG Preset C, available through the Nvidia App, significantly lowered latency versus the more compute-intensive Preset B. While input latency with Preset C is still high at about 84 ms, we have to take every bit of help we can get here, and the resulting 145 FPS average is notably smoother than native gameplay on my 160 Hz monitor.

    We only had time to dive into this one title in our testing, but when Nvidia says the RTX Spark platform is great for 1440p gaming, our experience suggests that you need to be ready to tweak DLSS upscaling and dial in MFG for more demanding games. And look: that’s fine. These are proven technologies at this point, and they let us get a better experience out of this platform than native rendering would allow.

    But all of these data points should go to show that if you're used to the low input latency and predictable performance scaling characteristics of an x86 desktop gaming PC with a discrete GPU, the RTX Spark platform still has a ways to go before it can truly replace such a system.

    During our AgentPerf-Local LLM benchmark, the EdgeMesa N AI+ pulls about 140 W from the wall, and under that load, it produces just 38.2 dBA at 18” (46 cm) according to our calibrated SPL meter, well below the 47.4 dBA of the RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra and the 48 dBA of the Ryzen AI Halo.

    That makes the EdgeMesa an easy system to live with for local AI work, especially if it’s moonlighting as an AI inference server or always-on agent host in shared spaces.

    Industry observers note that under gaming workloads, the EdgeMesa draws about 200 W. With more heat to dissipate, the MSI box’s noise output rises to 40.7 dBA, which is still much quieter than the average gaming laptop and will easily be covered by speakers or a closed-back gaming headset.

    The Ryzen AI Halo, on the other hand, emits a piercing 46.9 dBA whine while gaming, much closer to what we expect from a gaming laptop. And that’s not because it has that much more heat to dissipate; the AI Halo is pulling about 209 W with Control Resonant running.

    Under that same load, the EdgeMesa’s fans have a slightly high-pitched character to them, but it’s much less pronounced than the typical gaming laptop. Mostly, the sound from the system is that of air moving, and it's easy to ignore (so much so that I missed the aural cues I sometimes listen for when a benchmark finishes).

    MSI deserves high praise for this system’s thermal design and cooling system. It’s both quiet and pleasant-sounding, and those factors aren’t always a given with mini PCs.

    If you’re a hardcore Windows fan who’s been intrigued by Nvidia’s DGX Sparks for local AI, but you've been repelled by the idea of using Linux, RTX Spark desktops like this MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ finally pair your preferred OS with the same 6144-core Nvidia Blackwell GPU, 20-core Arm CPU, and up to 128GB of unified memory that give those systems their local AI grunt.

    These systems are a potentially exciting prospect for those who want to explore the possibilities of local AI and agentic workflows without the privacy and token caps of cloud models, all from the comfort of Windows.

    Recent findings suggest that but that potential comes with tradeoffs that you’ll need to weigh carefully before buying. And at an eye-popping $7,499 for the 128GB EdgeMesa configuration with a 4TB SSD that we tested, those tradeoffs weigh all the more heavily.

    Recent findings suggest that the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ delivers essentially the same performance from the RTX Spark N1X SoC (aka GB10) we’ve come to know and love for about a year now. It’s reasonably fast for local LLM inference, and it offers leading performance with generative AI workflows like images and videos in ComfyUI. Its Arm CPU offers solid enough single-threaded and multi-threaded performance for general computing tasks, and it can game in a pinch. The EdgeMesa is laudably quiet, too — no small feat for a compact PC like this.

    Recent findings suggest that but in exchange for Windows support, RTX Spark desktops lose the valuable expandability offered by the ConnectX 7 RDMA NIC that comes standard on DGX Spark boxes. So if you want to try your hand at running a bigger, more intelligent LLM than you can fit in one of these systems’ unified memory pools through clustering, you are forever out of luck if you go down the RTX path.

    Even if you can live without the ConnectX NIC, we’re a bit let down by the peripheral connectivity the EdgeMesa N AI+ offers, both for its price and for its ambitions as a do-it-all creator and gaming system.

    Recent findings suggest that with just three 20 Gbps USB Type-C ports on the back panel that have to do double duty as display outputs in multi-monitor setups, folks who have to juggle external storage and card readers frequently may find both the number and placement of those ports an obstacle to a smooth workflow. We really would have liked to see more expansion ports on this system overall, or at least one on the front panel.

    Nvidia loves to tout the gaming capability of Windows on Arm with RTX Spark systems, but we're still not that impressed by the experience in practice, especially for a system this expensive.

    Industry observers note that it's nice that you can enjoy PC gaming on these systems at all, but even in a desktop with more power and thermal budget to spare, the gaming performance and responsiveness we saw can only be described as adequate. We were especially surprised by the gulf in 1% low FPS between the RTX Spark and the much cheaper Ryzen AI Halo in Control Resonant, despite the RTX Spark N1X's much stronger GPU on paper.

    It has been revealed that in general, we find that it takes a lot of careful tweaking and application of DLSS magic to get around this platform's wrinkles for gaming (or a willingness to just let the Nvidia App optimize your game settings). In other words, don't retire your dedicated gaming PC or laptop just yet.

    In a recent development, the large memory pools available from RTX Spark systems have uses beyond local AI, of course. Nvidia GPUs are favorites for creative work on Windows, and if you work with massive 3D or game development projects, or you edit lots of high-resolution video, RTX Sparks are the first unified memory systems to pair a powerful Nvidia GPU with this much VRAM for Windows users.

    Adobe just updated several of its Creative Suite apps with Arm-native versions, so if you’re trying to blaze the trail of agentic content creation and generation in this modern age, an RTX Spark desktop (or laptop, for that matter) might be intriguing.

    But we feel like $7,499 is still a ton of money to spend on a system like this to run Adobe's apps specifically, unless a large unified memory pool is particularly useful for your work today.

    In a recent development, all told, we're left scratching our heads a bit about who RTX Spark desktops are really for. RTX Spark laptops meaningfully expanded the capabilities of mobile Windows on Arm systems thanks to the unmatched AI compute resources of their Blackwell GPUs and support for the full Nvidia software stack, along with solid CPU performance and battery life.

    But compared to both the existing DGX Spark platform and other mini PCs, RTX Spark desktops like the MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ ask you to give up a lot in exchange for the Nvidia-powered Windows on Arm experience, especially for the high prices they’re likely to command amid the current silicon supply crunch.

    If you’re a hardcore Windows-native developer or creator looking to explore the boundaries of what’s possible from local and agentic AI and want the best possible Microsoft-powered foundation for those activities, an RTX Spark desktop might be the right choice for the job, assuming you have the cash.

    But if you're just curious, we'd wait for the value proposition of local or agentic AI under Windows to firm up a bit and for the prices of these systems to come down before spending thousands of dollars on a still-fuzzy vision of the future of computing.

    As the Senior Analyst, Graphics at Tom's Hardware, Jeff Kampman covers everything that has to do with graphics cards, gaming performance, and more. From integrated graphics processors to discrete graphics cards to the hyperscale installations powering our AI future, if it's got a GPU in it, Jeff is on it.

    Breaking: Lawyer’s $9,450 private AI server with 12 used Nvidia V100s now runs every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that A lawyer has upped the ante by upgrading his private AI server from eight to 12 used Nvidia V100s, which can run every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert at 4-bit NVFP4.
    • Recent findings suggest that some of the best movie franchises come in threes, and Nick Mermiges seems determined to match that, taking his original setup — which he previously upgraded with more memory and other fixes — and expanding it for fuller precision, after a previous upgrade got him most of the way there.
    • According to recent reports, the original eight 32GB cards could manage 254 GiB, but the experts for the chosen model, with Nvidia’s NVFP4 release, need 278.9 GiB.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that A lawyer has upped the ante by upgrading his private AI server from eight to 12 used Nvidia V100s, which can run every DeepSeek V4.1 Flash expert at 4-bit NVFP4. Performance can reach up to 184 tokens per second for code, and long documents start answering in about half the time as before. He says it can outrun published DGX Spark stacks at decoding a single request, for half the price of three units, based on the $9,450 he paid.

    Recent findings suggest that some of the best movie franchises come in threes, and Nick Mermiges seems determined to match that, taking his original setup — which he previously upgraded with more memory and other fixes — and expanding it for fuller precision, after a previous upgrade got him most of the way there. The newest upgrade, this time, involves a third board of V100s, for a total of 12 with four per board. There may be a method to his madness.

    According to recent reports, the original eight 32GB cards could manage 254 GiB, but the experts for the chosen model, with Nvidia’s NVFP4 release, need 278.9 GiB. His previous workaround was to have every expert on the cards at 2-bit precision, with the most-used, 5,949 or about 38.7%, swapped to NVFP4 until the cards were full. Now, all 15,360 experts can live on the cards in their full glory, as he intended, with “none compressed further,” according to his GitHub repo. In a longer write-up on his site, he states the expert values “equal the ones in DeepSeek’s own release,” although other parts of the model use compact forms.

    A keen observer will notice a limitation of the V100s, which he spells out: the V100 has no FP4 or FP8 tensor cores. Every NVFP4 number has to be unpacked in software, first, and into half precision. The compact experts still pay off “because the cards read fewer bytes, not because they compute faster.” This helps explain why a card from 2018 can run a format from the Blackwell era.

    The model’s layers are, again, divided among the boards, this time with 0–13, 14–27, and 28–39, and each board’s section is split across its own four cards. The cards on a board share Nvidia’s fast link, or NVLink, and the hand-offs between boards cross over the host’s PCIe through two separate PCIe switches. The first two boards share a PEX88096 switch, so their hand-off stays inside it, but the third board is behind a separate PLX 8749, so the second hand-off also has to cross the host’s PCIe bridges, which adds latency.

    All this trouble is worth it, though, as with different settings — each card’s power cap raised from 150 W to 175 W and its clock cap lowered from 1,522 MHz to 1,452 MHz — there are noticeable improvements to performance as well as precision.

    His measurements show the first code token, with 256K context, at 58 seconds, almost twice as fast as the 108.4 seconds after his previous upgrade. Prompt reading is at “about 4,500 tokens a second” past 32K, which is more than twice the roughly 2,200 tokens a second of his first build, though the higher power cap likely accounts for some of that. Code decode, meanwhile, is 23% faster at 1K, but shows no real gains at 32K and up, so the real gain is a reduced wait for the first token.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    There was some eagerness to get more out of the system by pushing each card to 200 W for a day, but “the host tripped once under four long chats at once,” implying the power draw was perhaps too much. He also worked to optimize the setup as much as possible, but four optimizations — a conversation store that saves to disk, a leaner hand-off between sections, tighter expert packing, and exact four-card-sum arithmetic — had to be turned off due to missing their targets.

    Another common technique is to run multiple requests at once, usually netting a speed improvement. In this case, three requests at 128K got about 360 tokens per second in total on code and 213 on legal. That said, “this is not a batched-decode engine; more requests than sections gain little.”.

    Sources indicate that however, that might be next on the docket, as he looks to study batched decoding, “the one thing the Sparks have that I want,” he wrote on Reddit. Beyond that, there are plans to turn on the conversation store so a matter’s documents can survive a restart. While he acknowledges that the numbers do not establish “answer quality in use,” the setup has been his default DeepSeek machine since Monday, and he says the model is the first one “that works like Opus 4.6” for him.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A Bloomberg reporter was ejected from a historic trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China, and Russia after reportedly asking a sensitive question to the U.S.
    • Industry observers note that A second reporter had then started asking a second question before Chinese officials shushed the group.
    • Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation as the CEO of Nvidia has been a major scandal in the past few weeks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A Bloomberg reporter was ejected from a historic trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China, and Russia after reportedly asking a sensitive question to the U.S. President while in the presence of the leader of the Chinese Communist Party. According to The Washington Post, Bloomberg News journalist Annmarie Hordern, the chief political correspondent and co-host of the media outlet’s leading program, Bloomberg Surveillance, asked, “President Trump, has Jensen Huang been disloyal to the United States?”.

    Industry observers note that A second reporter had then started asking a second question before Chinese officials shushed the group. It’s unclear if Trump was able to answer both these questions. Senior White House Correspondent for Fox News Jacqui Heinrich mentioned on X that China, the host country of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit where the trilateral meeting was happening along the side, told journalists that “yelling questions is considered extremely rude” and that anyone doing so “will be pulled from the room,” possibly implying the nature of the questions' delivery, rather than its content, was behind the decision.

    Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation as the CEO of Nvidia has been a major scandal in the past few weeks. Even though he admitted to having an affair, he did not name the third party, reported to be Alice Huang, a Chinese executive for Megaspeed who’s also accused of diverting $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips into China and passing along information to Chinese intelligence.

    According to recent reports, the U.S. and China have been locked in a rivalry in recent years, with artificial intelligence being one of the industries that the Chinese Communist Party is focusing on. This race to achieve “supremacy” in AI has led the White House to impose export controls on its most powerful chips and to bar hardware containing U.S. tech from making its way into China. But even though Trump made a 180-degree turn and finally allowed Nvidia H100 chips into China in December 2025, provided the company can secure export licenses, the most advanced Blackwell and upcoming Vera Rubin chips from Nvidia are still out of reach for Chinese companies. Aside from that, Washington is also closing a loophole that allowed Chinese AI firms to take advantage of American compute by exporting their data to data centers located in other countries. Despite all those controls, rumors of AI chip smuggling still persist, with several individuals, including Supermicro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, getting arrested for chip diversion.

    It has been revealed that china also puts tighter control on its journalists and censors sensitive topics. As the host of the APEC summit and the trilateral meeting, it could exclude reporters that it thinks violate its standards. Heinrich said that the White House advocated for Hordern’s inclusion in the trilateral meeting, but it seems that the Chinese refused to budge on their decision.

    #70007. Breaking: 4 phases of becoming a great leader

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: 4 phases of becoming a great leader

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, below, Tony Martignetti shares four key insights from his upcoming book, Illuminating Hidden Brilliance: The Power of Multidimensional Leadership in a One-Dimensional World.
    • Below, Tony Martignetti shares four key insights from his latest book, Illuminating Hidden Brilliance: The Power of Multidimensional Leadership in a One-Dimensional World.
    • It has been revealed that martignetti is a leadership and workplace culture adviser, global keynote speaker, experience designer, and the host of The Virtual Campfire podcast.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, below, Tony Martignetti shares four key insights from his upcoming book, Illuminating Hidden Brilliance: The Power of Multidimensional Leadership in a One-Dimensional World. Martignetti is a leadership and workplace culture adviser, global keynote speaker, experience designer, and the host of The Virtual Campfire podcast. He began his career as a finance and strategy executive in the high-tech and life sciences industries before leaving the corporate world to help leaders integrate all of who they are into how they lead. What’s the Big Idea? The world does not need more exhausted leaders. It needs integrated and multidimensional leaders who can serve as lighthouses for others. If you are ready to stop fragmenting your brilliance and start illuminating it, then the four phases of Illuminating Hidden Brilliance are for you. Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Martignetti himself—in the Next Big Idea app, or buy the book. 1. Discover The first phase is about uncovering what’s been hidden. For decades, we’ve been sold a seductive story: focus narrowly, pick a lane, master one thing, and leave the rest of yourself at the door. That story made sense in the age of the assembly line, when problems were linear and predictable. That isn’t the world we’re leading in now. I lived this myself. Early in my career, I took pride in being “the numbers guy.” But my real breakthroughs never came from the spreadsheets alone. They came when I paired that analytical rigor with something more creative, like sketching visual maps or drawing metaphors that helped executives feel the strategy instead of just understand it. Now that AI has arrived, it could run those same models in seconds. But it is only able to replace the mechanical part of my contributions. What made me valuable was never the calculations. It was the ability to connect analysis with narrative and logic with imagination. Integration isn’t dilution; it’s differentiation. AI is the ultimate specialist. Our human edge is curiosity, empathy, intuition, creativity, and the ability to make meaning across boundaries. So how do you find what’s been hidden? One way is what I call Flashpoint Excavation. When I began interviewing guests on my podcast, I noticed a pattern. Every leader, whether a CEO, an artist, or a change maker, could trace their most significant growth to a single inflection point: a moment when the old story stopped working and a new one began. Those moments often came disguised as endings. But each one carried an ember of brilliance. When have you hidden a part of yourself to fit the mold of professional success? And what did it cost you? 2. Distill Not every dimension needs equal airtime. Distilling is about deciding what matters most, what wants expression now, and what deserves protection. The heart of this phase is learning to navigate polarities. Being multidimensional means living in constant tension: focus and freedom, logic and intuition, ambition and rest. We’re taught to pick a side and eliminate complexity. But these tensions aren’t flaws to fix. They’re the forces that shape growth. I once coached a healthcare executive who constantly wrestled with the tension between compassion and performance. When we mapped that polarity, she realized her empathy wasn’t softening her results. It was strengthening her influence. Her teams trusted her more deeply, which made accountability easier to sustain. When she stopped choosing between results and relationships, both grew stronger. I think of it like jazz. There’s a structure, a key, a beat, and within it, there’s improvisation. The music works because of the relationship between discipline and play. Leadership works the same way. One of my clients, Alina, keeps a simple note on her desk that reads, “Hold both ambition and humility lightly.” Whenever she feels herself slipping into all-or-nothing thinking, those words bring her back. Distilling also means finding your edge. When I left the corporate world, I thought freedom would be the reward. Instead, I found the chaos of too many possibilities. One morning, after weeks of trying to design the perfect business initiative, I closed my laptop, walked outside, and noted to myself, “I don’t need more space. I need better focus.” So, I ran a small experiment. I called it Campfire Conversations: intimate gatherings where leaders shared the stories behind their breakthroughs. That single experiment created a depth I could never have planned, and it became the foundation of my work. I call this the Edge Effect. Brilliance doesn’t happen in endless open space. It happens at the edges, where freedom meets form. 3. Design With clarity in place, the third phase is about designing the practices, rhythms, and environments that sustain your brilliance. This is where leadership becomes intentional instead of reactive. The first quality to design for is elasticity: the capacity to bend without breaking. I love the story of Lego. In the early 2000s, the organization was on the verge of collapse. It had expanded into video games, theme parks, fashion, and television. The problem wasn’t too little innovation. It was too much, too fast. When Jørgen Vig Knudstorp became CEO, he did two things that seemed contradictory. First, he set limits. He cut the number of unique pieces in half and guided every decision with one question: Does this build on the brick? Then he opened the doors wider than ever, inviting fans around the world to design new sets. Structure and imagination stopped being enemies and became dance partners. As he put it, “We needed to become smaller and bigger at the same time.” The second piece of Design is Presence Engineering. You cannot live in a multidimensional life with a one-dimensional operating system. Without intentional practices, expressing more of yourself can turn into scattered energy and role-switching fatigue. Presence Engineering gives you a through line that holds your whole identity, so you don’t lose yourself as you expand. When you design for integration, remarkable things can happen. Dina, a cardiac surgeon I once coached, told me privately, “I feel like a robot sometimes.” When I asked her the last time she’d lost herself in the moment, she quietly said, “When I used to paint.” She had hidden that part of herself for years. “You can’t be a serious surgeon and a painter,” she said. A few weeks later, she faced one of the most complex cases of her career. She stepped up to the table and saw the patient’s heart differently. “It looked like something I wanted to paint,” she told me. Her team later described her movement that day as fluid, and almost choreographed, and the surgery was a success. She designed small practices: sketching before difficult cases, taking two minutes outside before scrubbing in, and hanging her paintings in her office. Not only that, but she began telling her residents, “Technical precision saves lives, but your presence saves you.” 4. Deliver The final phase is about extending your integration outward into conversations, teams, organizations, and communities, so your leadership becomes a catalyst for collective brilliance. It often starts with a single conversation. I once worked with a global tech company that was six weeks from a major product launch, and every meeting felt like a battlefield. Engineering said the product wasn’t ready. Marketing said the messaging was unclear. Finance said the budget was already over. No one could see the whole picture. Then a quiet, mid-level product manager stepped in and said, “Before we talk about deliverables, let’s talk about realities. Paint me the picture of what you’re seeing.” Each group sketched its version of the problem on a whiteboard, and as they drew, a pattern appeared that everyone could finally see. Within two days, they’d redesigned the launch, and the product shipped on time. She didn’t solve their problems. What she did was build a bridge between their worlds. That’s the kind of leader the future needs: interpreters and bridge builders who design conversations where people feel seen. To sustain that impact over the long arc of a career, I come back to the image of a lighthouse. A lighthouse doesn’t shine in every direction with equal intensity. It doesn’t react to every wave passing. It stands rooted, and it rotates in a steady rhythm, and its light is focused, which is precisely why ships can steer by it. Think of Ernest Shackleton. In 1915, his ship, the Endurance, was trapped in Antarctic ice and eventually sank. He understood that the greatest danger to his crew was the slow erosion of hope. So he became their lighthouse, moving deliberately between roles: strategist, caretaker, challenger, and anchor, depending on what the moment required. His men later said they watched Shackleton more closely than the sun. Every single crew member survived. His brilliance wasn’t dramatic. It was disciplined. People rarely copy what leaders say. They copy who leaders are. When you model wholeness, you give others permission to bring theirs. The world doesn’t need more exhausted leaders shining endlessly in every direction. It requires integrated, multidimensional leaders who can shine steadily enough to guide others home. You don’t need to become louder, only clearer. And you don’t need to become someone new. You just need to let more of who you already are into the room. This article originally appeared in Next Big Idea Club magazine and is reprinted with permission. One morning, after weeks of trying to design the perfect business plan, I closed my laptop, walked outside, and said to myself, “I don’t need more space. I need better focus.”.

    So, I ran a small experiment. I called it Campfire Conversations: intimate gatherings where leaders shared the stories behind their breakthroughs. That single experiment created a depth I could never have planned, and it became the foundation of my work. I call this the Edge Effect. Brilliance doesn’t happen in endless open space. It happens at the edges, where freedom meets form.

    With clarity in place, the third phase is about designing the practices, rhythms, and environments that sustain your brilliance. This is where leadership becomes intentional instead of reactive.

    The first quality to design for is elasticity: the capacity to bend without breaking. I love the story of Lego. In the early 2000s, the firm was on the verge of collapse. It had expanded into video games, theme parks, fashion, and television. The problem wasn’t too little innovation. It was too much, too fast.

    Recent findings suggest that when Jørgen Vig Knudstorp became CEO, he did two things that seemed contradictory. First, he set limits. He cut the number of unique pieces in half and guided every decision with one question: Does this build on the brick? Then he opened the doors wider than ever, inviting fans around the world to design fresh sets. Structure and imagination stopped being enemies and became dance partners. As he put it, “We needed to become smaller and bigger at the same time.”.

    The second piece of Design is Presence Engineering. You cannot live in a multidimensional life with a one-dimensional operating system. Without intentional practices, expressing more of yourself can turn into scattered energy and role-switching fatigue. Presence Engineering gives you a through line that holds your whole identity, so you don’t lose yourself as you expand.

    When you design for integration, remarkable things can happen. Dina, a cardiac surgeon I once coached, told me privately, “I feel like a robot sometimes.” When I asked her the last time she’d lost herself in the moment, she quietly said, “When I used to paint.” She had hidden that part of herself for years. “You can’t be a serious surgeon and a painter,” she said.

    A few weeks later, she faced one of the most complex cases of her career. She stepped up to the table and saw the patient’s heart differently. “It looked like something I wanted to paint,” she told me. Her team later described her movement that day as fluid, and almost choreographed, and the surgery was a success.

    According to recent reports, she designed small practices: sketching before difficult cases, taking two minutes outside before scrubbing in, and hanging her paintings in her office. Not only that, but she began telling her residents, “Technical precision saves lives, but your presence saves you.”.

    The final phase is about extending your integration outward into conversations, teams, organizations, and communities, so your leadership becomes a catalyst for collective brilliance. It often starts with a single conversation.

    It has been revealed that I once worked with a global tech company that was six weeks from a major product launch, and every meeting felt like a battlefield. Engineering said the product wasn’t ready. Marketing said the messaging was unclear. Finance said the budget was already over. No one could see the whole picture.

    Recent findings suggest that then a quiet, mid-level product manager stepped in and stated, “Before we talk about deliverables, let’s talk about realities. Paint me the picture of what you’re seeing.” Each group sketched its version of the problem on a whiteboard, and as they drew, a pattern appeared that everyone could finally see. Within two days, they’d redesigned the launch, and the product shipped on time.

    According to recent reports, she didn’t solve their problems. What she did was build a bridge between their worlds. That’s the kind of leader the future needs: interpreters and bridge builders who design conversations where people feel seen.

    According to recent reports, to sustain that impact over the long arc of a career, I come back to the image of a lighthouse. A lighthouse doesn’t shine in every direction with equal intensity. It doesn’t react to every wave passing. It stands rooted, and it rotates in a steady rhythm, and its light is focused, which is precisely why ships can steer by it.

    In a recent development, think of Ernest Shackleton. In 1915, his ship, the Endurance, was trapped in Antarctic ice and eventually sank. He understood that the greatest danger to his crew was the slow erosion of hope. So he became their lighthouse, moving deliberately between roles: strategist, caretaker, challenger, and anchor, depending on what the moment required. His men later said they watched Shackleton more closely than the sun. Every single crew member survived.

    His brilliance wasn’t dramatic. It was disciplined. People rarely copy what leaders say. They copy who leaders are. When you model wholeness, you give others permission to bring theirs.

    Sources indicate that the world doesn’t need more exhausted leaders shining endlessly in every direction. It requires integrated, multidimensional leaders who can shine steadily enough to guide others home. You don’t need to become louder, only clearer. And you don’t need to become someone new. You just need to let more of who you already are into the room.

    #70006. SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve, but here’s how to care for elderly parents without upending your life

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3123 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

    SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve, but here’s how to care for elderly parents without upending your life

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that in its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues.
    • In its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues.
    • This sketch, starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that in its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues. But rarely has an SNL sketch resonated as deeply—and prompted as many national conversations—as the Sister commercial parody that aired on November 14, 2026. This sketch, starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents. The parody claims that simply texting the words “Dad fell” to your sister will prompt her to quit her job, break her lease, and completely upend her life to come take care of him—for free. Clearly, the all-male writing team of Streeter Seidell (who dedicated the sketch to his sister, Heidi), Mikey Day, Simon Rich, and Chase Rosenberg are onto something. AARP found that as of 2025, 59 million Americans were providing care for an adult loved one, and women made up 61% of those caregivers. And it’s taking a toll. AARP reports that caregivers of adults over 50 have been caregiving for 5 years and spend 26 hours per week providing care—up from an average of 3.9 years and 22 hours per week as of 2020. About 20% of those caregivers rate themselves as having fair or poor health, and they report an average of 7 poor mental health days per month. These unpaid caregivers spend an average of $11,508 per year on caretaking, which is equal to 31% of the median household income. Women across the country may have laughed through their rage at this painfully accurate comedy—but they deserve more than the mere satisfaction of simply feeling seen by an incisive satire. Cameron Huddleston, author of Mom and Dad, We Need to Talk, and Dr. Darla Bishop, financial wellness expert, public health researcher, and author of How to Afford Everything, offer the following practical suggestions for how America’s siblings can take care of aging parents without upending their lives, bankrupting themselves, or emptying their retirement accounts. Don’t minimize the costs of caregiving The humor of the SNL sketch relies on the family’s ignoring and downplaying the very real cost the sister pays when she becomes the caregiver. As Dr. Bishop puts it, “If you’re cutting back your hours, turning down promotions, or dipping into your retirement savings, caregiving has a price tag, even when no money changes hands.” But the sister faces more than just financial costs. We see her clash with her father and brother and argue with her husband. “In my work, I teach people to think about their three currencies: time, energy, and money,” Dr. Bishop claims. “Caregiving requires all three.” So rather than the sister being a free resource, as Mulaney claims in the ad, she’s using up all of her currencies while her brother pays nothing. Recognizing the heavy costs of caregiving is the first step to breaking the dynamic illustrated by SNL. “I want families to understand that just because you can afford to help your parents today doesn’t mean you can afford the long-term consequences of doing it alone,” Dr. Bishop says. Don’t ignore available resources “When a parent needs care, families assume they have two choices: do it themselves or pay someone else,” Dr. Bishop says. “But there are resources in between, and finding them could save your family thousands of dollars and countless hours.” Specifically, Dr. Bishop recommends starting with your local Area Agency on Aging, which can help you find services like transportation, meal delivery, respite care, and caregiver support. She also suggests exploring the Eldercare Locator at eldercare.acl.gov to help find affordable caregiving near you. You also don’t have to figure out these services on your own. According to Huddleston, an aging life care professional can help. (These people were previously known as geriatric care managers.) “These professionals will be familiar with resources in your area—from adult day care centers to government programs and community assistance,” Huddleston says. To find an aging life care professional, check out the Aging Life Care Association in your area. And don’t forget other, potentially overlooked resources available to you. Your parents may be eligible for Medicaid, depending on their income, health, and location. The VA’s Aid and Attendance program provides benefits for veterans and their spouses that help cover the cost of assistance with activities of daily living. Even your own employer benefits may help. “Some workplaces offer caregiver support, flexible scheduling, or access to care coordinators,” Dr. Bishop says. Don’t go it alone Huddleston was a caregiver for her mom, who had Alzheimer’s disease. One of her regrets about that time was not asking for more help from her family. “If I had asked, I would’ve gotten more help,” she says, “but I didn’t want to be a burden on others.” This gets to a common mindset the SNL skit illustrates: A lot of women are afraid to ask for help. “We assume it’s our responsibility, and we don’t want to appear like we can’t manage that responsibility,” Huddleston says. While it’s true that sometimes women ask for help and don’t receive it, Huddleston believes that many families assume the caregiver has it covered. “My husband was great about helping with my mom, doing so much to support me and her,” she says. “I’d love to see more men respond that way. But if they’re not seeing the toll it takes on the caregiver, as my husband saw daily with me, they probably aren’t even aware of how much of a sacrifice it is to care for a parent.” When asking for help, Dr. Bishop’s three currencies framework can help you figure out who can do what. You can divide responsibilities based on the time, energy, and money you each bring to the table. “Maybe one sibling lives nearby and can take Mom to appointments while another has more financial flexibility and can contribute toward paid care,” Dr. Bishop suggests. “A third might be great at managing paperwork, coordinating benefits, or researching resources.” Huddleston recommends keeping a running list of the types of support you need so that you’re prepared to make specific requests. “You might ask your brother to find an aging life care professional and cover the cost, to line up a housekeeper or lawn maintenance for your parents’ house, to pay for grocery delivery, to come stay with your parent in the evenings or weekends to give you a break,” she says. She also wants caregivers to let go of any guilt they have about asking for specific help. “It would be easier if men stepped up without being asked to help,” she says. “But if you’re not getting the help you need, don’t feel bad about asking for it.” Don’t wait to make decisions It’s easy to put off thinking about Mom and Dad’s health. None of us like to consider our parents’ mortality, and the idea of losing independence can be terrifying to an aging parent. But it’s easier to make good decisions before Dad falls, when no one is panicked or stressed. That’s why both Huddleston and Dr. Bishop both recommend having a family meeting well before there’s a crisis. “Put everything on the table,” Dr. Bishop says. “Ask yourselves, ‘What does our parent need? What resources do they already have? What can each of us realistically contribute without jeopardizing our own financial security?’” If your family tends to avoid such conversations, Huddleston suggests using the SNL skit as a jumping-off point to start the conversation. Don’t neglect your own long-term care planning Another way to break the cycle of relying on women’s unpaid caregiving is by planning for our own future care needs—and much earlier than you might think. “By the time you’re 50 years old, you should be thinking about long-term care and how you could pay for professional care so that you don’t have to rely entirely on a family member for support,” Huddleston says. “At that age (and into your early 60s if you’re healthy), you can still qualify for long-term care insurance or a hybrid life insurance policy with long-term care benefits.” Dr. Bishop also recommends getting your affairs in order—and that doesn’t just mean having a will in place. “One of the greatest gifts you can give your adult children is not making them play detective during a family crisis,” she says. Specifically, your kids should know where to find your important documents, who manages your money, what insurance you have, and your wishes in the event that you can’t make medical or financial decisions for yourself. So funny it hurts It’s unlikely that Saturday Night Live expected its three-minute parody to trigger a national reckoning about women’s disproportionate caregiving burden. But it struck a nerve for a very good reason. As Dr. Bishop puts it, “women aren’t the backup plan. We are THE PLAN.” But that doesn’t mean we’re stuck with this dynamic forever. We can end our reliance on women’s unpaid labor by recognizing the heavy time, energy, and money cost of caregiving; exploring all available resources; refusing to let one person handle all caregiving; making proactive decisions; and planning ahead for our own long-term care needs. “The answer isn’t for women to stop caring about their families,” Dr. Bishop says. “It’s for families to stop assuming that caring automatically equals sacrificing your career, your finances, or your own well-being.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Motorola’s Razr Flex has leaked in full, with the iPhone Duo competitor showing off its wide form factor in two colors, and it looks great.

    Following a leaker earlier this morning, SammyGuru has published newly introduced images of the Razr Flex, an iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor that Motorola has been teasing for months now.

    It has been revealed that these images show the “Dark Botanical Garden” green and “Coriander” brown with woven and leather-like backplates, two rear-facing cameras, and selfie cameras on both displays. The outer display, noted to be 4.97 inches, is wide but very compact, while the inner display is wide in the same way that the iPhone Duo is. The inner panel is expected to be around 7 inches in size.

    SammyGuru mentions that the hinge can hold itself half-open and that the price might come in at around $1,799 – though any guesses here are up in the air in the age of RAMageddon.

    Motorola Razr Flex is expected to launch in early 2027, with CES in January being a very likely launch timeline for the latest foldable.

    Tech Report: Thousands of vulnerable fridges patched against cyberattacks in secret operation

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, following devastating hacks that caused European fridges to reach 50 degrees Celsius, destroying food stocks, the UK has implemented nationwide patching to ensure similar attacks won't affect its fridges.
    • Refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions were the first to identify the concern before the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) all became involved in working on the problem.
    • Recent findings suggest that "From a business perspective, it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, following devastating hacks that caused European fridges to reach 50 degrees Celsius, destroying food stocks, the UK has implemented nationwide patching to ensure similar attacks won't affect its fridges. While it was thought that the UK had avoided similar hacks because it used different devices from those used in mainland Europe, an even worse issue was just waiting to be discovered. The BBC reports that a different flaw was discovered by security researchers in late October, one that could have caused even worse damage if it had been identified by hackers. Since then, work has been carried out to harden security across the U.K., with fridges in supermarkets, warehouses, and elsewhere now protected.

    Refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions were the first to identify the concern before the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) all became involved in working on the problem. As a precaution, thousands of devices that control tens of thousands of fridges were blocked from accessing the internet, with supermarket IT workers scrambling to sometimes physically isolate devices by removing network cables.

    Recent findings suggest that "From a business perspective, it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," one supermarket worker warned.

    According to recent reports, the concern that they were trying to address rested within the most popular refrigeration controllers used across the U.K., made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM). It was found that these controllers had a similar authentication security flaw to those hacked across Europe, although RDM points out that hacking its devices would have required a specific piece of hardware. However, that hardware is freely available.

    RDM has since confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on any of its controllers throughout the patching process.

    In a recent development, the situation in France, Belgium, and other European countries was much more dire. After initially hitting France in October, a further wave of attacks swept through supermarkets and even blood banks. Even the fridges at a U.S. military base were not safe.
